catholic.salvation: Catholics teach that salvation is God bringing people into friendship with himself and making them actually righteous, not only treating them as if they were. It begins with God's gift (grace), is received in baptism, and continues through faith, repentance, and good works. They speak of both salvation and justification. It is a process that can be lost by serious unrepented sin and restored by turning back to God.
evangelical.salvation: Evangelicals typically speak of being saved as a personal rescue by Jesus: God forgives sin and gives new life when a person trusts Christ. Many describe a definite turning point rather than only a lifelong process. Good works are expected as fruit of salvation, not as the way one first becomes saved.
lds.salvation: Latter-day Saints use salvation for rescue from death and sin through Jesus Christ, and often reserve exaltation for the highest future life with God, including becoming like him. Almost all people are said to be resurrected. The fullest blessing depends on faith, sacred rites, and enduring in covenant. The words do not map one-to-one onto a simple saved-versus-lost split.
ortho.salvation: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of salvation as healing and union with God, often called theosis (sharing in God's life without becoming God by nature). It is less a single courtroom verdict and more a lifelong cure. Faith, baptism, sacred rites, prayer, and love work together. Being saved as a one-time slogan is not their usual language.
evangelical.new_birth: Evangelicals use born again or new birth for an inner change when a person comes to living faith in Jesus. It means God gives a new spiritual life, not a second physical birth. Many treat it as the moment of conversion; some see it as the Spirit's work unfolding over time.
lds.christian_status: Latter-day Saints identify as Christians because they worship Jesus Christ as Son of God and Savior. They reject the idea that Mormon, an informal older nickname, means they are outside Christianity. Many other churches dispute that claim because LDS teaching about God and Scripture differs from the classical creeds. The debate is about the definition of Christian, not about whether Jesus is central in LDS life.
catholic.communion: Catholics call the central worship meal the Eucharist or Mass. They believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ while still looking like bread and wine. Communion is both a meal of thanksgiving and a making-present of Christ's one sacrifice. It is not treated as a mere symbol.
protestant.communion: Most Protestants call the meal the Lord's Supper or Communion. They remember Jesus' death with bread and wine or juice. Views range from a memorial sign to a real spiritual encounter with Christ. They generally do not use Mass as their ordinary name for the service.
catholic.trinity: Catholics teach the Trinity: one God in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—equal and eternal, not three gods and not one person wearing three masks. Person here means a distinct who, not a human personality.
christadelphian.trinity: Christadelphians reject the Trinity. They teach that God is one: the Father alone is the true God. Jesus is the human Son whom God raised up, not an eternal second person in God. The Spirit is God's power and presence, not a third person.
iglesia_ni_cristo.trinity: Iglesia ni Cristo teaches that there is one God, the Father. Jesus is the Christ and appointed Son, but not God in the same sense as the Father. They reject one God in three persons. The Holy Spirit is God's power, not a co-equal person.
jehovahs_witnesses.trinity: Jehovah's Witnesses reject the Trinity as unbiblical. Jehovah alone is the almighty God. Jesus is his first created Son, highly exalted but not equal to the Father. The holy spirit is God's impersonal active force, not a person.
lds.trinity: Latter-day Saints speak of the Godhead: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost as three distinct beings who are one in purpose, not one being. They do not use Trinity in the classical one-substance, three-persons sense.
oneness_pentecostal.trinity: Oneness Pentecostals reject three eternal persons. They teach Oneness: one God who reveals himself in different roles or manifestations—as Father, in the Son, and as Holy Spirit—with Jesus as the name and full revelation of that one God.
oriental_ortho.trinity: Oriental Orthodox churches confess the Holy Trinity: one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three persons, one essence. This matches the early creeds they accept. Their difference with other ancient churches is mainly about how Christ's humanity and divinity are described.
ortho.trinity: Eastern Orthodox Christians confess the Holy Trinity: one God in three hypostases (persons), the Father as source, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding from the Father. They stress both the unity of God and the real distinction of the three.
protestant.trinity: Most Protestants teach the Trinity: one God, three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the triune God. This follows the early creeds. A minority of groups from the Protestant world reject it; the mainstream does not.
unitarian.trinity: Unitarian Christians teach the unity of God: the Father alone is God. Jesus is usually honored as Messiah, teacher, or uniquely inspired human, not as a second person of one God. The classical Trinity is rejected as a later development.
catholic.father: Catholics call God the Father the First Person of the Trinity, the unbegotten source of the Son and Spirit. He is not a senior god above the others, nor merely a role.
jehovahs_witnesses.father: Jehovah's Witnesses identify the Father with Jehovah, the one almighty God. Jesus is his Son, not the same being. The Father is not a title shared equally by a Trinity of persons.
lds.father: Latter-day Saints speak of Heavenly Father, often Elohim, as a distinct exalted being, the Father of human spirits. Jesus is a separate being, his firstborn Son. This is not the classical one-substance Father.
oneness_pentecostal.father: Oneness Pentecostals treat Father as a title for the one God in his role as creator and source, not as a person distinct from Jesus. The same one God is Father in heaven and was manifested in the flesh as the Son.
ortho.father: Eastern Orthodox Christians call God the Father the unoriginate source of the Godhead: the Son is begotten of him and the Spirit proceeds from him. The Father is not God in a way that excludes the Son and Spirit from being fully God.
protestant.father: Protestants typically speak of God the Father or Heavenly Father as the first person of the Trinity, to whom prayer is often addressed through the Son. He is not a different god from Jesus, nor only a metaphor.
catholic.holy_spirit: Catholics teach that the Holy Spirit is the Third Person of the Trinity, also called the Paraclete (advocate or helper). He is fully God, not a force or mood. He gives life, holiness, and gifts in the Church.
jehovahs_witnesses.holy_spirit: Jehovah's Witnesses write holy spirit without treating it as a person. It is God's active force—his power at work—like energy sent from Jehovah, not a third divine person to be prayed to.
lds.holy_spirit: Latter-day Saints distinguish the Holy Ghost as a spirit personage in the Godhead from the gift of the Holy Ghost, a lasting right to the Spirit's companionship given after baptism by the laying on of hands.
oneness_pentecostal.holy_spirit: Oneness Pentecostals speak of the Holy Ghost or Spirit of God as the one God acting in power in believers, not as a third person beside the Father and Jesus. Receiving the Spirit is central to conversion experience.
ortho.holy_spirit: Eastern Orthodox Christians confess the Holy Spirit as fully God, the third person, who proceeds from the Father and is worshiped with the Father and the Son. He is the giver of life and the one who makes the Church holy.
pentecostal.holy_spirit: Pentecostals emphasize the Holy Spirit or Holy Ghost as a divine person who can fill believers with power, gifts, and a felt presence. This is more experiential language than many other Protestants use, but still Trinitarian in classical Pentecostalism.
protestant.holy_spirit: Protestants generally teach that the Holy Spirit, sometimes Holy Ghost in older English, is the third person of the Trinity, who inspired Scripture, gives new life, and dwells in believers.
catholic.filioque: Catholics teach the Filioque: the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. This phrase was added in the Latin creed. It means the Spirit's eternal coming-forth involves both Father and Son, not that there are two sources of God.
oriental_ortho.filioque: Oriental Orthodox churches teach that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, following the original creed. They do not accept the later Latin addition and the Son (Filioque) as part of the creed's wording.
ortho.filioque: Eastern Orthodox Christians insist the Spirit proceeds from the Father. They reject adding and the Son (Filioque) to the creed, seeing it as changing the Father's unique role as source.
protestant.filioque: Most Western Protestants inherited the Filioque and say the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Many treat it as a technical point about the Trinity rather than a daily slogan.
catholic.essence_and_energies: Catholics speak of the one divine essence (what God is) and of grace as a created gift in the soul, though they also say God gives himself. They do not usually divide God into essence versus uncreated energies the way many Orthodox writers do.
oriental_ortho.essence_and_energies: Oriental Orthodox speak of God's one nature and his operations or workings in the world. They affirm that God is truly known in his acts while remaining beyond full comprehension. They do not always use the later pair essence and energies.
ortho.essence_and_energies: Eastern Orthodox theology distinguishes God's essence (what God is in himself, which creatures never become) from his uncreated energies (God's real work and presence, such as uncreated light). People can share in the energies and thus truly meet God without becoming the divine essence.
jehovahs_witnesses.name_of_god: Jehovah's Witnesses treat Jehovah as the proper name of the one God, from the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH. Using the name is central to true worship. They argue many Bibles hide the name by printing LORD.
lds.name_of_god: Latter-day Saints use several names: Elohim often for the Father, and Jehovah typically for the premortal Jesus. God can mean the Father or the united Godhead. This mapping differs from churches that use Jehovah only for the Father or for the one Trinity.
messianic.name_of_god: Messianic believers often prefer Hebrew names: YHVH or Hashem (the Name) for God, and Yeshua for Jesus. This is about recovering Jewish forms, not usually about denying the New Testament Jesus. Practices vary by group.
oneness_pentecostal.name_of_god: Oneness Pentecostals emphasize the name of Jesus as the revealed name of the one God in the New Testament. Baptism and prayer in Jesus' name express that the fullness of God is known in Jesus.
catholic.incarnation: Catholics teach the Incarnation: the eternal Word, the Son, became flesh, a real human being, Jesus of Nazareth, without ceasing to be God. God the Son added a human nature; he did not turn into a mere man.
christian_science.incarnation: Christian Science distinguishes Christ, the divine idea or spiritual truth, from the human Jesus. Incarnation is not God taking a material body in the usual sense; matter is treated as unreal compared with Spirit. This does not map onto ordinary God-became-man language.
lds.incarnation: Latter-day Saints teach that the premortal Christ, Jehovah, was born on earth as Jesus, taking a mortal body. They speak of his mortal birth more than of one-person, two-natures formulas. He is divine and became truly human, while remaining a being distinct from the Father.
oriental_ortho.incarnation: Oriental Orthodox churches teach that the Word became flesh: the eternal Son took humanity and is one incarnate Lord. Their technical language about one nature after the union is meant to protect unity, not to deny that Jesus is fully human.
ortho.incarnation: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach the Incarnation or enfleshment of the Word: the Son became truly human while remaining truly God. This is the basis of worship, icons of Christ, and hope that humans can share God's life.
protestant.incarnation: Protestants typically teach that God became man: the eternal Son took a full human nature. Jesus is not a demigod or a good man later adopted as Son.
catholic.natures_of_christ: Catholics follow the Council of Chalcedon: Jesus is one person with two natures, fully God and fully man, united without mixing or splitting (the hypostatic union). He is not half-God, half-man, and not two people.
church_of_the_east.natures_of_christ: The Church of the East is dyophysite: it speaks of two natures and two qnome, a Syriac term for concrete individual realities, in the one Christ. This stresses that divinity and humanity remain distinct. They reject being labeled as teaching two sons or two Christs.
jehovahs_witnesses.natures_of_christ: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus is the created Son who lived as a perfect man. He is not God by nature in the same way Jehovah is. After death he was raised as a spirit creature, not as a God-man with two natures in the creed sense.
lds.natures_of_christ: Latter-day Saints teach that Jesus has divine and mortal natures: he is the divine Son who took a mortal body and inherited mortality through Mary. They do not typically use Chalcedon's one-person, two-natures vocabulary.
oneness_pentecostal.natures_of_christ: Oneness Pentecostals say God was manifest in flesh: the one God dwelt in the man Jesus. They often distinguish the deity from the humanity of Jesus rather than speaking of two eternal persons. Jesus is both fully God and fully man in their preaching.
oriental_ortho.natures_of_christ: Oriental Orthodox are miaphysite: they speak of one incarnate nature of the Word, meaning divinity and humanity united in one Christ. They reject mixing into a third thing and reject splitting Christ into two. One nature here does not mean he is not truly human.
ortho.natures_of_christ: Eastern Orthodox Christians accept Chalcedon: two natures in one person. Jesus is fully God and fully man. The natures are united without change, mixture, division, or separation.
protestant.natures_of_christ: Most Protestants teach that Jesus is fully God and fully man, two natures in one person, following the early councils. They reject both Jesus is only a man and Jesus only seemed human.
catholic.virgin_birth: Catholics teach the virgin birth or virginal conception: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit in Mary without a human father. This is about his origin, not a general rule for other births.
lds.virgin_birth: Latter-day Saints teach that Mary was a virgin and that Jesus' conception was divine, not ordinary human fatherhood. Official teaching affirms a real virgin birth of the Son of God.
ortho.virgin_birth: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach that Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, without a human father. The virgin birth is part of confessing who he is.
protestant.virgin_birth: Most historic Protestants teach that Jesus was born of a virgin: conceived by the Holy Spirit. Some modern Protestants treat it as optional or symbolic; classic Protestant confessions do not.
catholic.preexistence_of_christ: Catholics teach that the Son is the eternal Word, begotten of the Father before all time. He did not begin to exist at Christmas. Preexistence means eternal deity, not a previous created life as a human spirit.
christadelphian.preexistence_of_christ: Christadelphians teach that Christ came into being at his birth or conception. He is the promised Son, not an eternal second person who lived in heaven first. Old Testament texts about him are read as promise and plan.
jehovahs_witnesses.preexistence_of_chris: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus existed before Bethlehem as God's first creation, often identified with the archangel Michael. He is preexistent but not eternally uncreated.
lds.preexistence_of_christ: Latter-day Saints teach a premortal Christ: Jesus lived with the Father before birth as Jehovah, the firstborn spirit son. All humans also lived premortally as spirits. This is a previous personal existence, not only eternal God without beginning in the creed sense.
ortho.preexistence_of_christ: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach the eternal generation of the Son: begotten of the Father before all ages. The Son always was. Preexistence is eternal deity, not a created earlier career.
protestant.preexistence_of_christ: Mainstream Protestants teach the eternal Son or preexistent Christ: Jesus is the Word who was with God and was God before taking flesh. Groups that deny this are minorities relative to historic Protestantism.
catholic.atonement: Catholics teach that Christ's death is atonement and redemption: he makes satisfaction for sin and frees people from slavery to evil. The cross is a real saving act, explained with several images—sacrifice, victory, payment—not only one slogan.
christian_science.atonement: Christian Science reads atonement as at-one-ment: coming into unity with God by seeing the unreality of sin, sickness, and death as material error. It is not primarily a blood sacrifice that pays a legal debt.
lds.atonement: Latter-day Saints speak of the Atonement of Jesus Christ as including both Gethsemane, where he suffered for sins, and the cross, plus the resurrection. It makes repentance and resurrection possible. The garden is emphasized more than in many other churches.
ortho.atonement: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach atonement as redemption and often as Christus Victor: Christ defeats death, sin, and the devil and heals human nature. They are wary of reducing the cross to a punishment transferred onto Jesus in a strictly legal sense.
protestant.atonement: Many Protestants center the atonement on the cross and, in evangelical forms, on penal substitution: Jesus bears the penalty of sin in the place of sinners. Other Protestant voices stress moral example or victory over evil.
reformed.atonement: Reformed Christians typically teach penal substitution and, in classical forms, limited atonement: Christ actually secured salvation for the elect rather than only making it possible for all. The cross satisfies divine justice.
catholic.resurrection_of_christ: Catholics teach that Jesus truly rose from the dead as the risen Lord: the same crucified one lives bodily, not as a ghost or idea. Easter is the center of the faith.
lds.resurrection_of_christ: Latter-day Saints teach a literal resurrection of Christ: his body and spirit reunited, never to die, opening the way for all to be raised.
ortho.resurrection_of_christ: Eastern Orthodox Christians call Christ's rising Pascha (Easter): the defeat of death. The Resurrection is the heart of worship. It is a real bodily rising, not a metaphor.
protestant.resurrection_of_christ: Protestants teach the resurrection of Jesus and the empty tomb as historical saving events. Jesus lives bodily. Denying a real resurrection is outside classic Protestant confession.
catholic.ascension: Catholics teach the Ascension: the risen Jesus entered heaven as man and remains there, still the same Jesus, until he returns. It is not disappearing into myth.
lds.ascension: Latter-day Saints teach that the risen Christ ascended and continues his work, including later appearances described in their additional scripture.
ortho.ascension: Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate the Ascension as Christ taking glorified human nature into the life of God and sitting at the Father's right hand. Humanity is thereby honored.
protestant.ascension: Protestants teach the ascension of Christ: Jesus returned to the Father's presence and reigns. From there he sends the Spirit and will come again.
lds.offices_of_christ: Latter-day Saints speak of the roles of Christ as Creator, Savior, Judge, and head of the Church, among others. They do not always use the Protestant slogan prophet, priest, and king, though those ideas appear in other words.
protestant.offices_of_christ: Many Protestants summarize Jesus' work as prophet, priest, and king, the threefold office: he reveals God, offers himself and intercedes, and rules. It is a teaching outline, not a third nature.
reformed.offices_of_christ: Reformed theology names this the munus triplex, the threefold office of Christ as prophet, priest, and king. Each office explains a side of his saving work and present role.
catholic.gifts_of_the_spirit: Catholics speak of gifts of the Holy Spirit and charisms: some are lasting habits of holiness, others are special abilities for service. Gifts are for building up the Church, not for private status.
lds.gifts_of_the_spirit: Latter-day Saints teach that gifts of the Spirit such as healing, prophecy, tongues, and discernment continue in the Church when faith is present. They are signs of God's work, not proof that every claimant is true.
ortho.gifts_of_the_spirit: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of charismata, gifts of the Spirit, given in the life of the Church, especially through the sacraments and holiness. Spectacular gifts are not the usual test of a Christian.
pentecostal.gifts_of_the_spirit: Pentecostals emphasize spiritual gifts as present and expected, often listing nine gifts from 1 Corinthians 12. They are tools of mission and worship for today.
protestant.gifts_of_the_spirit: Protestants teach spiritual gifts as abilities the Spirit gives for service. Traditions disagree about whether dramatic gifts such as tongues and healing still operate as in the New Testament.
catholic.baptism_in_the_spirit: In Catholic charismatic renewal, baptism in the Spirit means a later stirring or release of the Spirit already given in baptism and confirmation. It is not a replacement for the sacraments.
evangelical.baptism_in_the_spirit: Many evangelicals speak of being filled with the Spirit as empowerment for holy living and witness. They often do not treat it as a required second stage proved by tongues.
holiness.baptism_in_the_spirit: Holiness churches often speak of entire sanctification or a second blessing: a distinct work of God after conversion that cleanses the heart and empowers love. Some link this with Spirit baptism; not all require tongues.
lds.baptism_in_the_spirit: Latter-day Saints speak of the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost as the Spirit's cleansing and confirming work that should follow water baptism, typically connected with confirmation and laying on of hands.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spiri: Oneness Pentecostals treat Holy Ghost baptism, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues, as essential to the full new-birth pattern along with repentance and Jesus-name baptism.
pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spirit: Classical Pentecostals teach baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience after conversion that empowers witness, typically first shown by speaking in tongues.
catholic.tongues: Catholics recognize a gift of tongues as one possible charism: prayer or speech in a language unknown to the speaker, to be used in order and tested. It is not required of every Catholic.
oneness_pentecostal.tongues: Oneness Pentecostals treat tongues as the usual biblical evidence that a person has received the Holy Ghost. Without that sign, they typically do not say the Spirit baptism has occurred.
pentecostal.tongues: Pentecostals teach speaking in tongues, glossolalia, as the common initial evidence of Spirit baptism, and as a gift for prayer and sometimes for a message with interpretation.
protestant.tongues: Protestants disagree. Some accept tongues as a gift of languages or prayer speech; others say the New Testament gift was real languages for the apostolic age only. Many Protestant churches never practice it.
reformed.tongues: Classic Reformed teaching is often cessationist about tongues: the sign gift of languages served to launch the gospel and has ceased. Ongoing glossolalia is treated with suspicion or as something other than the New Testament gift.
catholic.continuationism: Catholics teach that charisms continue in the Church. Miracles and special gifts are possible, though they are tested by authority and not treated as a new public revelation equal to Scripture.
evangelical.continuationism: Evangelicals are split on the charismatic question: whether sign gifts such as tongues, prophecy, and healing continue. Some are continuationist, some cessationist, many cautious in between.
pentecostal.continuationism: Pentecostals are continuationist: the gifts are for today, not only for the first century. A church without room for gifts is seen as missing New Testament life.
reformed.continuationism: Many Reformed churches teach cessationism: the cluster of sign gifts ceased with the apostles and the finished New Testament. God still heals and guides, but not through a standing gift of apostles and tongue-speakers as then.
reformed_baptist.continuationism: Reformed Baptists commonly hold cessationism similar to other Reformed Christians: the founding sign gifts have ceased, and Scripture is sufficient for guidance now.
catholic.justification: Catholics teach justification as God making a person righteous, infused righteousness, not only counting them righteous. It begins in baptism, grows, and can be lost and restored. Faith is necessary but is not faith alone in the Reformation slogan sense.
lds.justification: Latter-day Saints use justification for being made right or pardoned through Christ as one cooperates in covenant. It is tied to faith, repentance, and ordinances, and is not usually isolated as a one-time legal declaration only.
ortho.justification: Eastern Orthodox Christians can say justification, meaning being made righteous, but they fold it into the larger healing of salvation. They do not typically center a forensic, courtroom-only declaration the way many Protestants do.
protestant.justification: Classic Protestants teach justification as being declared righteous by God through faith, on the basis of Christ—imputed righteousness, credited, not infused as a quality one then merits by. Good works follow; they do not cause this verdict.
reformed.justification: Reformed Christians stress justification by faith alone and forensic justification: a legal verdict that the sinner is righteous in Christ. It is distinct from the later growth called sanctification.
catholic.sanctification: Catholics teach sanctification as growth in holiness by grace, inseparable from justification in living practice. Becoming holy is real change, not only a new label.
holiness.sanctification: Holiness churches teach entire sanctification or Christian perfection: a work of God that can cleanse the heart from the ruling power of sin in this life, producing perfect love. Perfection means mature love, not flawless skill in every act.
lds.sanctification: Latter-day Saints teach sanctification as being made more holy through Christ's atonement, obedience, and the Spirit. It is a process tied to covenants and endurance.
methodist.sanctification: Methodists speak of going on to perfection or Christian perfection: growth into love that fills the heart. Wesleyan teaching allows a distinct crisis of sanctification as well as gradual growth.
ortho.sanctification: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach sanctification as part of theosis: becoming holy by sharing God's life. It is liturgical, disciplined, and communal, not a separate legal stage only.
protestant.sanctification: Protestants teach sanctification as being made holy after or alongside justification: the Spirit changes character over time. Most deny that this process is finished in this life in an absolute sense.
catholic.glorification: Catholics speak of glorification as the final completion of salvation, including the beatific vision: seeing God face to face in heaven, and the resurrection of the body.
lds.glorification: Latter-day Saints often use exaltation, eternal life, or celestial glory for the highest outcome: living in the Father's presence, continuing family bonds, and becoming like God. Glorification in Protestant usage only partly overlaps.
protestant.glorification: Protestants use glorification for final redemption: resurrection, freedom from sin, and life with God. It is the last step after justification and sanctification.
catholic.theosis: Catholics speak of divinization or becoming partakers of the divine nature: sharing God's life by grace without becoming a member of the Trinity. The idea is present, though theosis is more an Eastern word.
lds.theosis: Latter-day Saints teach exaltation: the faithful may become like God, including a glorified, embodied life and, in fullest teaching, creative and parental likeness to him. This goes beyond what Catholics and Orthodox mean by theosis.
oriental_ortho.theosis: Oriental Orthodox teach theosis or deification: humans are meant to share in God's life and glory through Christ, remaining creatures. It is union, not identity of essence.
ortho.theosis: Eastern Orthodox Christians make theosis central: becoming partakers of the divine nature by the energies of God. People become godlike by grace, never God by nature.
protestant.theosis: Some Protestants speak of union with Christ or even deification in a modest sense: sharing Christ's life and likeness. Most avoid language that sounds like humans become gods.
catholic.grace: Catholics distinguish sanctifying grace, a share in God's life that makes one holy, from actual grace, help for particular acts. Grace is a gift, yet people must freely cooperate. It is more than a mere change of legal status.
lds.grace: Latter-day Saints teach grace as Christ's enabling gift. A well-known Book of Mormon phrase says people are saved by grace after all we can do, meaning grace is essential and effort is expected, not that one earns heaven unaided.
ortho.grace: Eastern Orthodox Christians often call grace uncreated: it is God himself at work, divine energies, not only a created thing poured into the soul. Grace heals and deifies.
protestant.grace: Protestants typically define grace as unmerited favor: God's kindness to the undeserving. Emphasis falls on gift, not on a substance stored in the soul.
reformed.grace: Reformed Christians speak of sovereign grace: God freely gives salvation to those he chooses, and this grace effectively brings them to faith. Human cooperation does not originate the gift.
catholic.faith_and_works: Catholics teach faith working through love: living faith includes trust and deeds. Works done in grace are part of how justification is lived and increased, not a rival currency beside Christ.
churches_of_christ.faith_and_works: Churches of Christ stress obedient faith: trust that does what the gospel commands, including baptism for forgiveness. They reject both faith with no obedience and salvation by earning.
lds.faith_and_works: Latter-day Saints teach that faith and works belong together: trust in Christ, ordinances, and enduring to the end. Neither slogan faith alone nor earn your way fits their official balance.
ortho.faith_and_works: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach synergy: God acts and humans freely respond. Faith and works are two sides of one living response, not a contest between trust and effort.
protestant.faith_and_works: Classic Protestants teach sola fide, faith alone, as the instrument of justification, while insisting that real faith produces works. The dispute with Catholics is about what justifies, not about whether Christians should do good.
catholic.predestination: Catholics teach predestination to glory in the sense that God foreknows and prepares the saved, without teaching that he creates anyone for hell apart from their sin. Human freedom remains real.
methodist.predestination: Methodists typically teach conditional election: God chooses those who respond to prevenient grace, help given before conversion that restores ability to believe. They reject unconditional predestination to salvation or damnation.
ortho.predestination: Eastern Orthodox Christians emphasize God's foreknowledge more than a decree that overrides freedom. Predestination language is used cautiously so that synergy and responsibility remain.
protestant.predestination: Protestants disagree among themselves. Some teach strong divine choosing; others teach that predestination follows foreseen faith. The word itself only means that God has a purpose about people's final end.
reformed.predestination: Reformed Christians teach unconditional election: God chooses some for salvation not because he foresaw their faith, but of his own purpose. This is the sharpest classic form of predestination among Protestants.
catholic.election: Catholics speak of election as God's choosing a people and calling persons to salvation, compatible with free response. It is not usually a list of individuals fixed without regard to how they live and repent.
lds.election: Latter-day Saints speak of election and also foreordination: God assigned missions in the premortal life. This is not the same as irresistible Calvinist election; agency remains.
protestant.election: Protestants use election for God's choosing of a people or of individuals in Christ. Meanings range from God chose whoever would believe to God chose particular people to believe.
reformed.election: Reformed Christians speak of the elect as those God chose for salvation before they did anything good or bad. Election is the cause of faith, not its reward.
baptist.perseverance: Many Baptists teach eternal security or once saved, always saved: a truly converted person will not be finally lost. Practice varies between no one who believed can be lost and those who fall away show they were never truly saved.
catholic.perseverance: Catholics teach that perseverance is a gift. A justified person can commit mortal sin and lose grace. Final salvation is hoped for, not treated as an unlosable possession in this life.
evangelical.perseverance: Many evangelicals teach once saved always saved or eternal security. Others in the evangelical family, especially Wesleyan, say a believer can walk away. The slogan is common but not universal.
lds.perseverance: Latter-day Saints teach that one must endure to the end in covenant. Salvation in the fullest sense is not a locked status after a single prayer.
methodist.perseverance: Methodists historically teach that a person can fall from grace by willful unbelief and sin. Security is found in remaining in Christ, not in an unbreakable once-for-all certificate.
reformed.perseverance: Reformed Christians teach perseverance of the saints: those truly chosen and regenerated will be kept by God and will endure. Apparent dropouts were not truly converted, or they will be restored.
catholic.assurance: Catholics generally teach hope of salvation rather than absolute certainty of one's final destiny, apart from rare special revelation. One may be confident of being in grace now without claiming infallible knowledge of the end.
evangelical.assurance: Evangelicals often emphasize knowing you are saved: inner witness, promises of Scripture, and a conversion story give assurance. Doubt is treated as a pastoral problem to be answered with gospel promises.
ortho.assurance: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak more of trust and hope than of a settled certificate of assurance. The aim is humble confidence in God's mercy while continuing repentance.
reformed.assurance: Reformed teaching includes assurance of faith as possible and desirable, grounded in God's promises, the Spirit's witness, and the fruit of a changed life—not in a passing feeling only.
catholic.repentance: Catholics teach repentance with contrition, sorrow for sin, confession, and a purpose to change. For serious sin after baptism this is tied to the sacrament of Reconciliation.
lds.repentance: Latter-day Saints teach repentance as recognizing sin, confessing, forsaking it, making restitution where possible, and turning to Christ. It is repeated and practical, not only an opening prayer.
oneness_pentecostal.repentance: Oneness Pentecostals treat repentance as the first step of the new-birth pattern: turning from sin toward God, followed by Jesus-name baptism and receiving the Spirit.
ortho.repentance: Eastern Orthodox Christians call repentance metanoia: a change of mind and heart, ongoing for life. It is practiced in confession, prayer, and turning from the passions, disordered desires.
protestant.repentance: Protestants teach repentance as turning from sin to God, paired with faith. It is inward change that shows itself in a new way of life.
catholic.means_of_grace: Catholics treat the sacraments as primary means of grace: appointed rites through which God gives the life he promises. Prayer, Scripture, and works of mercy also convey help.
lutheran.means_of_grace: Lutherans teach that God gives grace through the means of grace: the Word, preached and read, and the sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, and they also speak of confession. Faith clings to these outward promises.
methodist.means_of_grace: Methodists list means of grace such as prayer, Scripture, fasting, the Lord's Supper, and Christian fellowship. God ordinarily meets people through these practices.
protestant.means_of_grace: Protestants use means of grace for the usual channels God uses—especially Scripture, prayer, and the sacraments or ordinances. They deny that the rites work like magic apart from faith.
reformed.means_of_grace: Reformed churches teach Word and sacrament as means of grace: God truly gives Christ through preaching, baptism, and the Lord's Supper to those who believe, by the Spirit.
catholic.original_sin: Catholics teach original sin: humans inherit a fallen condition from Adam, lacking original holiness and inclined to sin. Baptism remits original sin. They do not teach that infants are personally guilty in the same way as actual sins they commit.
lds.original_sin: Latter-day Saints teach the Fall of Adam and Eve as a necessary step that made mortality and choice possible. They reject inherited guilt for Adam's transgression; children are not condemned for it. The Fall still brings death and a natural man that must be overcome.
oriental_ortho.original_sin: Oriental Orthodox speak of ancestral sin or the fall: death and corruption spread to the race. They emphasize inherited mortality and weakness more than inherited courtroom guilt.
ortho.original_sin: Eastern Orthodox Christians prefer ancestral sin: we inherit death, corruption, and a bent toward sin from Adam, not Adam's personal guilt as such. The problem is sickness and death as much as legal blame.
protestant.original_sin: Protestants teach original sin as a fallen condition affecting all people: guilt and corruption from Adam, so that humans need grace from the start. Strength of wording varies by tradition.
reformed.original_sin: Reformed theology teaches original sin with federal headship: Adam acted as representative, so his guilt and corruption are imputed to his descendants. Humans are unable to turn to God without regenerating grace.
catholic.human_nature: Catholics teach that human nature is wounded by sin—weakened in will and intellect, inclined to concupiscence, disordered desire—but not destroyed. People remain able to cooperate with grace.
lds.human_nature: Latter-day Saints speak of the natural man as an enemy to God unless yielded to the Spirit, yet they also teach that humans are spirit children of God with real capacity to choose good.
ortho.human_nature: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach that humans remain in the image of God after the fall, though the likeness, mature holiness, is damaged. Nature is sick, not totally worthless.
protestant.human_nature: Protestants generally teach a fallen nature: humans are bent away from God and cannot save themselves. How complete that inability is depends on the branch.
catholic.image_of_god: Catholics teach the imago Dei: every human bears God's image and therefore has dignity. Sin wounds the image; grace restores and perfects it.
lds.image_of_god: Latter-day Saints teach that humans are in God's image and are his spirit children, so the likeness is both moral and, in some sense, kindred. Embodiment is part of the divine plan, not a punishment only.
ortho.image_of_god: Eastern Orthodox Christians distinguish image, the given capacity for God, and likeness, the fulfilled holiness. The image remains after the fall; the likeness must be restored in theosis.
protestant.image_of_god: Protestants teach the imago Dei as the human calling to represent God. Sin distorts the image; in Christ it is renewed. They rarely use the Orthodox image/likeness pair as a technical system.
catholic.free_will: Catholics teach that free will remains after the fall, though weakened. Grace heals and helps the will; it does not replace it. People can accept or refuse grace.
lds.free_will: Latter-day Saints make agency or free agency central: the ability to choose is a gift of God and a purpose of mortal life. Foreordination does not cancel real choice.
methodist.free_will: Methodists teach free will restored by prevenient grace: God enables everyone to respond. Without that prior help, they agree humans would not turn to God; with it, refusal is possible.
ortho.free_will: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach free will and synergy: salvation is God's work with a willing human partner. The will is weakened but not destroyed.
protestant.free_will: Protestants disagree. Some teach significant freedom to accept the gospel; others teach that the will is bound in spiritual things until God gives new birth. All agree humans make real choices in ordinary life.
reformed.free_will: Reformed Christians speak of bondage of the will in salvation: apart from grace, people will not choose God. They may still speak of free agency in the sense that people choose according to their desires.
catholic.mortal_and_venial_sin: Catholics distinguish mortal sin, serious sin done with knowledge and consent that breaks friendship with God, from venial sin, lesser faults that wound but do not destroy that friendship.
ortho.mortal_and_venial_sin: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of sin and the passions rather than a strict mortal/venial legal pair. Some sins are soul-destroying if unrepented; all sin is treated as sickness to be healed.
protestant.mortal_and_venial_sin: Most Protestants do not use mortal versus venial as official categories. They may speak of willful sin versus weakness, but any sin is serious, and they reject a system of classifying which sins kill grace in the Catholic way.
catholic.total_depravity: Catholics reject the phrase total depravity if it means humans can do no good at all or have no remaining freedom. They teach a wounded nature and concupiscence: inclination to sin, not the destruction of the image of God.
ortho.total_depravity: Eastern Orthodox Christians explicitly reject total depravity as Reformed theology states it. Nature is corrupted and mortal, but humans still bear the image of God and can respond to him with help.
protestant.total_depravity: Some Protestants teach strong fallenness or inability in spiritual things; others soften it. Total depravity in popular speech is often confused with people are as wicked as possible, which even Reformed teachers usually deny.
reformed.total_depravity: Reformed Christians teach total depravity or total inability: every part of the person is affected by sin, so no one turns to God without regenerating grace. It does not mean every person is equally criminal.
catholic.scripture: Catholics call the Bible Sacred Scripture: the inspired written Word of God. It is read within the Church's tradition and teaching office, not as the only authority standing alone.
christian_science.scripture: Christian Science reads the Bible together with Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures by Mary Baker Eddy as the pastor and interpretive key. The second book functions as a companion authority, not a typical commentary.
lds.scripture: Latter-day Saints have standard works: the Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, and Pearl of Great Price, plus living prophetic teaching. Scripture is a larger set than the Protestant Bible alone.
ortho.scripture: Eastern Orthodox Christians honor Holy Scripture as inspired and central, always read inside Holy Tradition, the living faith of the Church. The Bible is not an isolated handbook.
protestant.scripture: Protestants call the Bible Scripture or the Word of God and treat it as the highest written authority for faith and life. How they relate it to creeds and pastors varies, but the Bible is the court of appeal.
catholic.canon: Catholics include the deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and additions to Daniel and Esther) in the Old Testament canon. Their Bible is larger than the usual Protestant 66-book Bible.
lds.canon: Latter-day Saints have an open canon in principle: God can add scripture. The standard works are the current bound set, and new revelation can be added by prophetic authority.
oriental_ortho.canon: Oriental Orthodox churches have canons that include books beyond the Protestant 66, with some variation by national church. Scripture is received in the Church's traditional list.
ortho.canon: Eastern Orthodox churches use a broader Old Testament, including books sometimes called anagignoskomena, worthy to be read. Exact lists can vary slightly by local church, but all are wider than the Protestant canon.
protestant.canon: Protestants typically hold a 66-book Bible: 39 Old Testament books matching the Hebrew canon and 27 New Testament books. Extra books may be read as history but are not used to prove doctrine.
anglican.sola_scriptura: Anglicans classically appeal to Scripture, tradition, and reason. Scripture is supreme, but it is read with the early church and thoughtful interpretation, not as a bare private text.
catholic.sola_scriptura: Catholics reject Scripture alone. They teach Scripture and Tradition as two streams of one revelation, interpreted by the Church's teaching office. The Bible is essential and inspired, but not a standalone court that overrides the Church.
lutheran.sola_scriptura: Lutherans teach sola scriptura: Scripture is the only final rule that can bind conscience and establish doctrine. Creeds and confessions are honored as faithful witnesses, not as equal sources beside the Bible.
ortho.sola_scriptura: Eastern Orthodox Christians reject Scripture alone. Holy Scripture lives inside Holy Tradition: liturgy, councils, fathers, and the mind of the Church. The Bible is not interpreted as a private, isolated authority.
protestant.sola_scriptura: Protestants teach sola scriptura, Scripture alone, as the highest authority for faith and practice. Other authorities exist, but they must be tested by the Bible. This does not mean no creeds, pastors, or history; it means none of those equals Scripture.
reformed.sola_scriptura: Reformed Christians strongly affirm sola scriptura. Confessions summarize the Bible but may be revised by it. Nothing may be required as necessary to salvation that Scripture does not teach.
catholic.inspiration: Catholics teach that Scripture is inspired, God-breathed: God is the author through human writers. Inspiration covers the books the Church receives as canonical.
lds.inspiration: Latter-day Saints teach that Scripture is inspired, but inspiration is not limited to a closed ancient list. Prophets and additional books can also be inspired Scripture.
ortho.inspiration: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach that Holy Scripture is inspired by God and true. Inspiration is understood within the Church that received and reads the books.
protestant.inspiration: Protestants teach that the Bible is inspired, often speaking of verbal inspiration: God so guided the writers that what they wrote is God's Word. Details of how that works vary.
catholic.inerrancy: Catholics teach that Scripture teaches saving truth without error. Modern official language often ties inerrancy to the truth God wished to put in the sacred writings for the sake of salvation, which interpreters debate in scope.
evangelical.inerrancy: Many evangelicals teach inerrancy: Scripture, in the original writings, is without error in all that it affirms, including history and fact, not only spiritual lessons. Infallibility is a closely related word.
ortho.inerrancy: Eastern Orthodox Christians affirm the truth of Scripture. They do not usually organize the debate under the modern Protestant word inerrancy, but they reject treating the Bible as a merely human, mistaken book.
protestant.inerrancy: Protestants commonly speak of the infallibility of Scripture: it does not fail as God's rule for faith. Some insist on full inerrancy; others limit reliability to matters of faith and morals.
anglican.apocrypha: Anglicans historically read the Apocrypha in church for example of life and instruction of manners, but not to establish doctrine. The books sit in a middle status unlike the Catholic deuterocanon or a purely rejected extra.
catholic.apocrypha: Catholics call these books deuterocanonical, second-canon, not Apocrypha in a dismissive sense. They are fully Scripture: Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and parts of Daniel and Esther.
ortho.apocrypha: Eastern Orthodox Christians include deuterocanonical books or anagignoskomena in their Bibles and liturgical reading. They are Scripture in church use, even if ranking discussions exist among some writers.
protestant.apocrypha: Protestants usually call these books the Apocrypha: valuable as historical or moral reading, not canonical Scripture for proving doctrine. They are omitted from most Protestant pew Bibles.
catholic.open_canon: Catholics teach a closed canon: the list of biblical books is finished. Private revelations may help devotion but cannot add books to the Bible or change public doctrine.
community_of_christ.open_canon: Community of Christ, from the Latter Day Saint movement, treats the canon as open in principle and continues to use the Book of Mormon and additional texts, with a different official stance from the LDS Church on many later revelations.
lds.open_canon: Latter-day Saints teach an open canon: God still speaks, so additional scripture such as the Book of Mormon can be added. The standard works can grow when the Church accepts new revelation.
protestant.open_canon: Protestants teach a closed canon: the 66 books are complete. No new book can stand beside them as Scripture, even if they believe God still guides the church.
seventh_day_adventist.open_canon: Seventh-day Adventists hold the biblical canon as closed, yet give a unique place to Ellen G. White's writings as the Spirit of Prophecy: a continuing gift that illuminates Scripture but is not a second Bible in theory.
catholic.continuing_revelation: Catholics teach that public revelation ended with the apostles. Private revelation, visions and locutions, may occur but cannot add to the deposit of faith. They must be tested by the Church.
lds.continuing_revelation: Latter-day Saints teach continuing revelation through living prophets. God still gives binding guidance to the whole church, not only personal impressions.
new_apostolic.continuing_revelation: The New Apostolic Church teaches continuing apostleship: living apostles still receive and transmit what the church needs. Revelation did not stop in the first century.
pentecostal.continuing_revelation: Pentecostals believe prophecy can occur today as a gift. Most still say it must be tested by Scripture and is not a new Bible. The accent is on present speech from God, not a closed silence.
protestant.continuing_revelation: Most Protestants teach closed revelation and the sufficiency of Scripture: God does not add new public doctrine after the New Testament. Guidance continues through Scripture and the Spirit, not through new canonical oracles.
seventh_day_adventist.continuing_revelat: Seventh-day Adventists teach a continuing prophetic gift, historically in Ellen G. White, called the Spirit of Prophecy. It is meant to apply and unfold Scripture for the last days, not to replace the Bible.
catholic.hermeneutics: Catholics teach that interpretation of Scripture belongs finally to the Magisterium, the Church's teaching office, in harmony with Tradition. Private reading is encouraged but not the last court of meaning.
ortho.hermeneutics: Eastern Orthodox Christians interpret Scripture in the Church, with the consensus of the Fathers and the liturgy as guides. Isolated private interpretation is distrusted.
protestant.hermeneutics: Protestants emphasize hermeneutics, methods of interpretation, and historically defended the right of believers to read Scripture. In practice churches still use confessions, scholars, and pastors as guides.
reformed.hermeneutics: Reformed Christians interpret Scripture by the analogy of faith: clearer passages interpret harder ones, and no reading may contradict the Bible's overall teaching as summarized in their confessions.
anglican.tradition: Anglicans honor tradition as a guide alongside Scripture and reason. Early councils and common prayer shape belief, but tradition is not treated as an independent equal in the Roman Catholic sense.
catholic.tradition: Catholics teach Sacred Tradition or Apostolic Tradition as the living handing-on of the gospel beside Scripture. It is not mere custom; it is part of how revelation reaches the present Church.
oriental_ortho.tradition: Oriental Orthodox churches live by Holy Tradition: liturgy, fathers, canons, and custom as the Church's memory of the apostles. Scripture is inside that stream.
ortho.tradition: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of Holy Tradition as the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church. It includes Scripture, councils, liturgy, icons, and the fathers as one whole, not a rival add-on to the Bible.
protestant.tradition: Protestants treat tradition as human inheritance that may be helpful or harmful. It must be judged by Scripture. Some traditions are kept; none is infallible simply by being old.
catholic.magisterium: Catholics teach the Magisterium, the teaching office of pope and bishops, as the living authority that interprets Scripture and Tradition. It is not a third revelation, but the authorized interpreter.
ortho.magisterium: Eastern Orthodox Christians do not have a single papal magisterium. They speak of the mind of the Church and the consensus of the Fathers, expressed in councils and the shared faith of the bishops and people.
protestant.magisterium: Protestants generally deny a centralized infallible teaching office. Teaching authority exists in pastors, confessions, and scholarship, but it remains reformable by Scripture.
catholic.papal_primacy: Catholics teach papal primacy: the pope, as successor of Peter and bishop of Rome, has a real governing and teaching primacy in the whole Church, often called the Petrine ministry.
old_catholic.papal_primacy: Old Catholics reject the First Vatican Council's account of papal primacy and jurisdiction. They may honor Rome historically while denying universal papal government over every local church.
oriental_ortho.papal_primacy: Oriental Orthodox churches do not accept Roman papal primacy as defined by later Catholic councils. Each church has its own patriarch or catholicos. Rome is not their court of final appeal.
ortho.papal_primacy: Eastern Orthodox Christians may grant the bishop of Rome a primacy of honor among ancient patriarchs, first among equals in the old order, but they reject later papal claims of universal jurisdiction.
protestant.papal_primacy: Protestants typically reject papal primacy as a binding doctrine. The papacy is treated as a historical office of the church of Rome, not as Christ's appointed head of all Christians.
catholic.papal_infallibility: Catholics teach papal infallibility: when the pope speaks ex cathedra, from the chair, defining a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church, he is preserved from error. It is a narrow, rare claim, not that every papal remark is perfect.
old_catholic.papal_infallibility: Old Catholics rejected papal infallibility when it was defined in 1870. That rejection is a founding mark of their separation from Rome.
ortho.papal_infallibility: Eastern Orthodox Christians reject papal infallibility. They locate the Church's reliability in conciliar agreement and the whole Church's faith, not in one bishop's defining voice.
protestant.papal_infallibility: Protestants reject papal infallibility as unbiblical and historically disproved in their view. No single office is guaranteed freedom from error in doctrine.
catholic.ecumenical_councils: Catholics recognize twenty-one ecumenical councils, from Nicaea to Vatican II. These assemblies of bishops, received by the pope, can define doctrine for the whole Church.
church_of_the_east.ecumenical_councils: The Church of the East classically receives the first two councils, Nicaea and Constantinople, and does not accept later councils such as Ephesus and Chalcedon in the same way as other ancient churches.
oriental_ortho.ecumenical_councils: Oriental Orthodox churches receive three ecumenical councils: Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus. They do not accept Chalcedon as ecumenical in the same sense.
ortho.ecumenical_councils: Eastern Orthodox Christians receive seven ecumenical councils, from Nicaea I to Nicaea II. Later Western councils are not binding on them.
protestant.ecumenical_councils: Protestants often honor the early councils, especially the first four, insofar as they agree with Scripture. They do not treat a later list of twenty-one, or even seven, as automatically binding apart from the Bible.
anglican.apostolic_succession: Anglicans claim apostolic succession: their bishops stand in a historic line of laying on of hands from the apostles. How necessary this is for a true church is debated within Anglicanism.
catholic.apostolic_succession: Catholics teach apostolic succession: bishops receive their office in a historic chain from the apostles, and this is required for the fullness of the Church and valid holy orders.
lds.apostolic_succession: Latter-day Saints teach a restored priesthood succession and apostolic authority. They hold that the ancient line was lost in a falling away and had to be given again by heavenly messengers.
oriental_ortho.apostolic_succession: Oriental Orthodox churches teach apostolic succession through their bishops and patriarchs. Valid ministry is tied to this historic handing-on of office.
ortho.apostolic_succession: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach apostolic succession as the handing-on of episcopal office and the apostolic faith. A chain of hands without the Orthodox faith is not treated as sufficient.
protestant.apostolic_succession: Many Protestants deny that a historic chain of bishops is required. Apostolic succession may mean continuity of apostolic teaching rather than an unbroken episcopal pedigree.
lds.prophetic_authority: Latter-day Saints teach that the President of the Church is a living prophet who holds priesthood keys for the whole church. Current prophetic teaching guides the church alongside scripture.
new_apostolic.prophetic_authority: The New Apostolic Church centers authority in apostles, headed by a Chief Apostle. This living apostolate is treated as necessary for the church's fullness.
pentecostal.prophetic_authority: Some Pentecostals recognize an office of prophet in a fivefold ministry pattern. Authority is usually local or networked and must be tested; it is not the same as an LDS church president.
seventh_day_adventist.prophetic_authorit: Seventh-day Adventists give unique weight to Ellen G. White as a bearer of the Spirit of Prophecy. Her writings guide interpretation and practice, while the Bible remains the stated final standard.
catholic.priesthood_authority: Catholics teach sacred power in Holy Orders: ordained bishops, priests, and deacons act in Christ's name in ways the unordained cannot, especially in the sacraments.
lds.priesthood_authority: Latter-day Saints teach priesthood keys in two orders, Aaronic and Melchizedek. Authority to perform ordinances must be conferred by laying on of hands from those who hold it.
ortho.priesthood_authority: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach that priesthood is a gift of the Holy Spirit given in ordination. Bishops, priests, and deacons serve the mysteries; authority is sacramental and conciliar.
protestant.priesthood_authority: Protestants speak of ministerial authority as service under the Word. Ordination sets people apart to preach and pastor, but it is not usually a separate sacred power in the Catholic sense.
catholic.church: Catholics speak of the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ, a visible communion with the successor of Peter. It is both a people and a structured society.
lds.church: Latter-day Saints speak of the Church as the restored organization of Jesus Christ, with prophets and apostles. They often mean their specific church when they say the Church.
ortho.church: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of the Church as a communion of local churches sharing the same faith, sacraments, and episcopacy. The Church is a visible eucharistic community, not only an idea.
protestant.church: Protestants speak of the church as the body of Christ: all who belong to Jesus, and also local congregations and denominations. Visible structures vary widely.
restorationist.church: Restorationists aim at the New Testament church: a return to first-century pattern rather than inherited denominations. The church is defined by going back to the original model.
catholic.one_true_church: Catholics teach that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church. Other Christians may have elements of truth and sanctification, but the fullness of the one true Church is identified with the Catholic communion.
churches_of_christ.one_true_church: Churches of Christ often say they are simply the church of Christ, not a denomination. The true church is those who follow the New Testament pattern of name, worship, and organization.
iglesia_ni_cristo.one_true_church: Iglesia ni Cristo teaches that it is the Church of Christ, the true church outside of which salvation is not found in their official teaching. Other churches are not recognized as the Lord's church.
lds.one_true_church: Latter-day Saints teach that theirs is the only true and living church, meaning the only church with the fullness of priesthood authority and saving ordinances, while acknowledging good in other faiths.
ortho.one_true_church: Eastern Orthodox Christians identify the one holy catholic and apostolic Church with the Orthodox Church. Others may be Christians in some sense, but the Church itself is the Orthodox communion.
protestant.one_true_church: Many Protestants distinguish an invisible church of all true believers from visible denominations. No single earthly organization is simply identical with the one true church.
adventist.great_apostasy: Adventists speak of a falling away in Christian history, especially the rise of unbiblical traditions and Sunday in place of Sabbath. They see themselves as a remnant calling the world back.
catholic.great_apostasy: Catholics reject a total Great Apostasy. They teach the indefectibility of the Church: it cannot fail as a whole or lose the gospel, even if members and ages are sinful.
jehovahs_witnesses.great_apostasy: Jehovah's Witnesses teach a great apostasy after the apostles, in which true teaching was corrupted until their modern restoration of pure worship.
lds.great_apostasy: Latter-day Saints teach the Great Apostasy: after the apostles, priesthood authority and fullness of the gospel were lost from the earth until the Restoration through Joseph Smith.
ortho.great_apostasy: Eastern Orthodox Christians deny that the Church failed. Local disasters and heresies occurred, but the Church as such did not disappear or need reinventing.
restorationist.great_apostasy: Restorationists generally teach an apostasy or falling away from the New Testament pattern, which their movement seeks to repair by returning to the Bible's church order.
catholic.marks_of_the_church: Catholics list four marks: one, holy, catholic, and apostolic. These describe the Church as united, set apart, universal, and founded on the apostles, visible in the Catholic Church.
ortho.marks_of_the_church: Eastern Orthodox Christians confess the same four marks. They apply them to the Orthodox Church as the one holy catholic and apostolic Church.
protestant.marks_of_the_church: Many Protestants, especially Lutheran and Reformed, name marks such as the pure preaching of the Word and the right administration of the sacraments, sometimes adding discipline. Unity under the pope is not a mark.
catholic.visible_and_invisible_church: Catholics emphasize the visible Church: a concrete communion with sacraments and shepherds. They do not deny that God knows hidden hearts, but they resist splitting church into an invisible true group and a visible shell.
ortho.visible_and_invisible_church: Eastern Orthodox Christians insist the Church is visible: you can point to her liturgy, bishops, and faith. An invisible-only church is rejected as a Protestant idea.
protestant.visible_and_invisible_church: Protestants commonly distinguish the invisible church, all the truly saved known to God, from the visible church, mixed congregations of believers and mere members.
reformed.visible_and_invisible_church: Reformed theology classically teaches both a visible and an invisible church. The elect form the church in God's sight; local churches are mixed bodies that must preach and discipline.
anglican.polity: Anglicans use episcopal polity: the church is governed by bishops, with priests and deacons, usually alongside synods. Bishop is a standing office, not only a local job title.
baptist.polity: Baptists typically use congregational government: the local church, under Christ, decides its membership, officers, and doctrine. Associations exist but do not rule parishes from above.
catholic.polity: Catholics use episcopal polity with a hierarchy: pope, bishops, priests, deacons. Authority is structured from the top of the college of bishops with and under the pope.
congregational.polity: Congregational churches vest government in the gathered local membership. Wider fellowships advise; they do not command the congregation as a bishop or presbytery would.
ortho.polity: Eastern Orthodox churches practice conciliarity or synodality: bishops govern together in synod, with a patriarch or metropolitan as first among them, not as a universal pope.
presbyterian.polity: Presbyterians use presbyterian polity: the church is governed by elders in graded courts—session, presbytery, general assembly—not by a single bishop or by majority vote of all members on every issue.
protestant.polity: Protestants use several systems of church government: episcopal, presbyterian, and congregational are the main families. Polity means how the church is organized and who decides.
baptist.local_church: Baptists treat the local church as an autonomous congregation of baptized believers. The local body, not a denomination headquarters, is the basic church.
catholic.local_church: Catholics organize daily life in a parish, a local community under a pastor, within a diocese under a bishop. The parish is not independent of the wider Catholic Church.
churches_of_christ.local_church: Churches of Christ stress the local congregation as independent, with no official denominational headquarters. Each congregation is the church in that place.
protestant.local_church: Protestants all have local churches, but they disagree about how free those congregations are from regional or national structures.
amish.church_discipline: The Amish practice Meidung, shunning: a member who breaks church rules and will not repent is avoided in social and table fellowship to bring about repentance and protect the community.
anabaptist.church_discipline: Anabaptists historically practiced the ban: exclusion from fellowship for unrepentant sin. Discipline is part of being a believers' church, not optional etiquette.
catholic.church_discipline: Catholics use excommunication and other canonical penalties. These restrict access to sacraments and legal standing; they aim at conversion and protection of the community, not mere punishment.
lds.church_discipline: Latter-day Saints use membership councils that can result in restrictions or excommunication. The goal is repentance and protection of the church's integrity.
protestant.church_discipline: Protestants historically practiced church discipline, including rebuke and excommunication. Practice today ranges from careful process to almost none, depending on the denomination.
catholic.ecumenism: Catholics pursue ecumenism as work for Christian unity, speaking of separated brethren. They seek closer ties without treating all differences as unimportant or all churches as equal in fullness.
evangelical.ecumenism: Evangelicals often prefer cooperation among those who share a gospel core rather than institutional merger. Ecumenism can mean partnership in mission, or it can be viewed with suspicion if doctrine is diluted.
ortho.ecumenism: Eastern Orthodox Christians are divided about ecumenism. Official dialogues exist, but many insist unity requires return to Orthodox faith and worship, not a federation of disagreements.
protestant.ecumenism: Protestants have been major drivers of modern ecumenism, seeking Christian unity across denominations. Some pursue organic union; others settle for friendship and shared projects.
catholic.schism: Catholics define schism as refusing communion with the pope or with members of the Church subject to him. It is a break in visible unity, distinct from heresy, which is a break in doctrine.
ortho.schism: Eastern Orthodox Christians treat schism as breaking eucharistic communion and canonical ties. A group may keep similar rites and still be schismatic if it leaves the canonical church.
protestant.schism: Protestants speak of schism or division as the fracturing of Christian fellowship. They often blame earlier corruption for making separation necessary, while still lamenting splits among themselves.
adventist.restoration: Adventists see themselves as a remnant people restoring neglected biblical truths, especially Sabbath and last-day teaching, rather than inventing a new religion.
churches_of_christ.restoration: Churches of Christ belong to the Restoration Movement: restore the New Testament church in name, baptism, worship, and organization, without creeds or denominational machinery.
lds.restoration: Latter-day Saints call their origin the Restoration: God restored lost priesthood, ordinances, and church structure through Joseph Smith after the Great Apostasy.
restorationist.restoration: Restorationists in general aim to restore the New Testament church. The method is going back to the Bible's pattern rather than reforming an existing historic church only in part.
baptist.ordination: Baptists practice ordination as the local church's public recognition of a person called to ministry. It is important, but not usually a sacrament that confers a new sacred character.
catholic.ordination: Catholics treat ordination as Holy Orders, a sacrament that confers a sacred character and power for ministry. Bishops confer it by laying on of hands.
lds.ordination: Latter-day Saints confer priesthood by ordination and also set people apart to specific callings by laying on of hands. Authority must be traced to those who hold keys.
ortho.ordination: Eastern Orthodox Christians call ordination cheirotonia, laying on of hands. It is a holy mystery that makes a man bishop, priest, or deacon within the Church.
protestant.ordination: Protestants practice ordination as setting apart ministers to preach and pastor. Meanings range from a sacrament-like rite to a simple commissioning.
catholic.priesthood: Catholics distinguish the ministerial priesthood of the ordained from the common priesthood of all the baptized. The ordained priest offers the Eucharist in a way the laity do not.
lds.priesthood: Latter-day Saints speak of priesthood as God's authority, organized as Aaronic and Melchizedek priesthoods, conferred on worthy males in current official practice, with distinct offices.
ortho.priesthood: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach an ordained priesthood that serves the holy mysteries. All the baptized share in a royal priesthood, but liturgical presidency belongs to the ordained.
protestant.priesthood: Protestants emphasize the priesthood of all believers: every Christian has direct access to God. Ordained ministers are servants of the Word, not a separate sacrificing caste.
anglican.episcopacy: Anglicans retain bishops as a historic and, for many, essential office. A bishop oversees a diocese, confirms, and ordains.
catholic.episcopacy: Catholics teach that bishops have the fullness of Holy Orders. They are successors of the apostles in office, shepherds of dioceses, and members of a worldwide college with the pope.
methodist.episcopacy: Many Methodist bodies have bishops who supervise clergy and conferences. The office is often more functional and connectional than a claim of historic apostolic succession in the Catholic sense.
ortho.episcopacy: Eastern Orthodox Christians treat the bishop, episkopos, as essential. There is no local church in the full sense without a bishop; he is the center of unity and Eucharist.
protestant.episcopacy: Some Protestants keep bishops; others read bishop as another name for pastor or overseer in the New Testament and do not create a third rank above elders.
baptist.elders: Some Baptist churches have a plurality of elders or treat pastor and elder as the same office. Others have a single pastor and a board of deacons instead of a formal eldership.
lds.elders: Latter-day Saints use elder as an office in the Melchizedek priesthood. Many adult men are elders; it is not only the title of a senior pastor.
presbyterian.elders: Presbyterians distinguish ruling elders, who govern, from teaching elders, ministers who preach. Together they form the session that leads the congregation.
protestant.elders: Protestants widely recover the New Testament word elder for church leaders. Whether elders and pastors are one office or two, and whether they rule a region, varies.
reformed.elders: Reformed churches are governed by elders. The eldership, not a single bishop and not a pure democracy, bears responsibility for doctrine and discipline.
baptist.deacons: Baptists typically have deacons as servants who handle practical care and sometimes share leadership. In many churches deacons function almost as a board; in others they strictly serve.
catholic.deacons: Catholics have deacons, including a permanent diaconate: ordained men, often married, who preach, baptize, and serve charity, but do not preside at Mass as priests do.
lds.deacons: Latter-day Saints confer the office of deacon on young men in the Aaronic priesthood. It is an entry office of service, not a late-career rank.
ortho.deacons: Eastern Orthodox deacons assist in the liturgy, chant litanies, and serve the bishop and priest. The office is ancient and liturgical, not merely administrative.
protestant.deacons: Protestants generally treat deacons as servants of mercy and administration. Some traditions make the office more liturgical; others more practical.
catholic.papacy: Catholics call the pope the Supreme Pontiff and Bishop of Rome, visible head of the Church on earth as successor of Peter. The papacy is a permanent office, not a honorary title.
ortho.papacy: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of the Pope of Rome as the bishop of an ancient and important see. They do not accept him as universal supreme pontiff over the Orthodox churches.
protestant.papacy: Protestants view the papacy as the leadership office of the Roman Catholic Church. They do not accept the pope as head of all Christians by divine right.
baptist.priesthood_of_believers: Baptists link the priesthood of believers with soul competency: each person stands before God and may read Scripture and believe without a priestly mediator. This supports congregational freedom.
catholic.priesthood_of_believers: Catholics affirm the common priesthood of the faithful given in baptism, while insisting it differs in kind from the ministerial priesthood of the ordained.
lds.priesthood_of_believers: Latter-day Saints speak of a general or widespread priesthood among worthy male members rather than only a professional clergy. This is not the same slogan as Protestant priesthood of all believers, because authority still must be conferred.
protestant.priesthood_of_believers: Protestants teach the priesthood of all believers: every Christian may come to God through Christ, offer spiritual sacrifices, and serve. This was a Reformation protest against a mediating priestly caste.
catholic.clerical_celibacy: In the Latin Catholic Church, priests normally live under clerical celibacy: they do not marry. This is a discipline, not an unchangeable dogma, but it is firmly established practice.
eastern_catholic.clerical_celibacy: Eastern Catholic churches, united with Rome, often allow married men to be ordained priests, while bishops are chosen from the celibate. This differs from the usual Latin rule.
ortho.clerical_celibacy: Eastern Orthodox churches ordinarily ordain married men as parish priests. Bishops are taken from the monastic, celibate clergy. Priests may not marry after ordination.
protestant.clerical_celibacy: Protestants reject mandatory clerical celibacy. Ministers may marry. Celibacy can be a personal gift, not a condition of ordination.
lds.apostles_today: Latter-day Saints have a Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and a First Presidency. They teach that living apostles hold the same kind of authorizing keys as the New Testament Twelve.
new_apostolic.apostles_today: The New Apostolic Church is built around living apostles as a continuing office necessary for sealing and church leadership.
pentecostal.apostles_today: Some Pentecostals teach a fivefold ministry that includes apostles today: pioneering, network-founding leaders. Others use the word loosely for missionaries. It is not usually a single worldwide quorum.
protestant.apostles_today: Most historic Protestants teach that the apostolic age ended: the Twelve and Paul were unique foundation stones. There are missionaries and church planters, but not apostles of that same office.
baptist.baptism: Baptists practice believer's baptism by immersion: a person who already believes is dipped in water as a public act of obedience and identification with Christ, not as the automatic cause of new birth in their usual teaching.
catholic.baptism: Catholics teach Baptism as a sacrament that washes original sin, gives new life, and incorporates a person into the Church. It is ordinarily necessary for salvation and is given to infants as well as adults.
churches_of_christ.baptism: Churches of Christ teach baptism for the remission of sins: immersion of a believing person is the appointed moment when God forgives and adds one to the church. Faith without this baptism is not treated as complete obedience.
lds.baptism: Latter-day Saints baptize by immersion those accountable, from age eight. It is a covenant ordinance for remission of sins and entrance into the church, performed by priesthood authority.
