oneness_pentecostal.baptism: Oneness Pentecostals insist on baptism in Jesus' name by immersion as part of the saving pattern, not the Trinitarian formula Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
ortho.baptism: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach holy baptism as a sacrament of death and rising with Christ, usually by triple immersion, given to infants and adults, followed at once by chrismation and communion.
protestant.baptism: Protestants all practice baptism with water in the triune name, but they disagree about infants, about whether it works regeneration, and about whether immersion is required.
anabaptist.infant_baptism: Anabaptists reject infant baptism and baptize only those who confess faith, credobaptism. Sixteenth-century Anabaptists were named for rebaptizing people already baptized as infants.
baptist.infant_baptism: Baptists practice believer's baptism only. Infant baptism is not accepted as New Testament baptism; those baptized as infants are baptized again upon profession of faith.
catholic.infant_baptism: Catholics baptize infants because they believe grace and membership in the Church are gifts a child can receive. Parents and godparents vow to raise the child in the faith.
lutheran.infant_baptism: Lutherans baptize infants, teaching that God gives promised grace even to children through this means. Faith is created by the Word in the rite, not postponed until adult understanding.
ortho.infant_baptism: Eastern Orthodox Christians baptize infants as full members of the Church and immediately chrismate and commune them. Baptism is not delayed until a later age of reason.
reformed.infant_baptism: Reformed churches practice covenant baptism of infants of believing parents. Children of the covenant receive the sign as circumcision once did, while personal faith remains necessary as they grow.
baptist.mode_of_baptism: Baptists insist on immersion: the person goes under the water. Pouring or sprinkling is not accepted as the proper New Testament mode.
catholic.mode_of_baptism: Catholics allow pouring or immersion. Validity depends on water and the Trinitarian formula with right intention, not on full submersion alone.
oneness_pentecostal.mode_of_baptism: Oneness Pentecostals baptize by immersion in Jesus' name. Both the mode and the spoken formula matter in their teaching.
ortho.mode_of_baptism: Eastern Orthodox Christians normally use triple immersion, once at each name of the Trinity. Other modes may be used in emergency, but immersion is the norm.
protestant.mode_of_baptism: Protestants disagree about mode. Some require immersion; many accept sprinkling or pouring as valid baptism if water and the name of God are used.
anglican.confirmation: Anglicans practice Confirmation: a bishop lays hands on the baptized who confess the faith, praying for strengthening by the Spirit. It is an important rite of mature belonging.
catholic.confirmation: Catholics teach Confirmation as a sacrament that completes baptismal grace, seals with the Spirit, and equips for witness. A bishop is the ordinary minister.
lutheran.confirmation: Lutherans practice Confirmation as a time of instruction and public confession after infant baptism. It is important pastorally; they do not always call it a sacrament in the Catholic sense.
oriental_ortho.confirmation: Oriental Orthodox churches practice Chrismation, anointing with holy oil, immediately after baptism. It is the gift of the Spirit, not a teenage graduation years later.
ortho.confirmation: Eastern Orthodox Christians call this Chrismation and give it with baptism, even to infants. It is the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.
protestant.confirmation: Some Protestants keep confirmation as a class and vow after infant baptism; others have no such rite because they baptize only believers.
anglican.confession: Anglicans allow confession to a priest as a ministry of forgiveness, while also teaching that confession directly to God is always possible. Practice ranges from rare to regular.
catholic.confession: Catholics teach Reconciliation, Confession, or Penance as a sacrament: after baptism, serious sins are confessed to a priest, who pronounces God's forgiveness. Regular confession is encouraged.
ortho.confession: Eastern Orthodox Christians practice the Mystery of Repentance: confession before a priest, who offers prayer of forgiveness. It is medicine for the soul, often tied to spiritual guidance.
protestant.confession: Protestants teach confession of sins to God, and often to one another, but most reject a required priestly sacrament of penance. Some Lutheran and Anglican churches retain a form of private confession.
catholic.anointing_of_the_sick: Catholics celebrate Anointing of the Sick, once commonly called Extreme Unction. Oil and prayer ask for healing, strength, and forgiveness for those seriously ill or aged, not only the dying.
ortho.anointing_of_the_sick: Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate Holy Unction: anointing with oil for healing of soul and body. It may be given in a communal service, not only at the point of death.
pentecostal.anointing_of_the_sick: Pentecostals practice anointing with oil and prayer for healing, following James 5. It is an act of faith for present healing, not a last rite.
protestant.anointing_of_the_sick: Some Protestants anoint the sick with oil as a biblical practice of prayer. Others simply pray without oil. Few treat it as one of seven sacraments.
anglican.holy_orders: Anglicans retain Holy Orders as bishop, priest, and deacon. Whether these orders are a sacrament in the Catholic sense is answered differently across Anglicanism.
catholic.holy_orders: Catholics teach Holy Orders as a sacrament that makes men deacons, priests, or bishops. It confers a lasting sacred character.
ortho.holy_orders: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach Holy Orders as a mystery conferring the offices of deacon, priest, and bishop. Ordination is an act of the Church by the Spirit.
protestant.holy_orders: Many Protestants speak simply of ordination rather than Holy Orders as a sacrament. Ministry is a calling and office under the Word.
catholic.matrimony: Catholics teach Matrimony as a sacrament: the marriage of two baptized persons is a sign of Christ and the Church and gives grace for the bond. The spouses are the ministers of the rite.
lds.matrimony: Latter-day Saints distinguish civil marriage from temple marriage or sealing, which they believe can bind a couple and family beyond death when covenants are kept.
ortho.matrimony: Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate the Mystery of Marriage with crowning of the couple. Marriage is a holy mystery of union, not only a contract.
protestant.matrimony: Protestants honor Christian marriage as instituted by God, but most do not list it among two gospel sacraments. It is a covenant before God and witnesses.
baptist.sacraments: Baptists prefer ordinances: baptism and the Lord's Supper as commanded memorial acts of obedience, not channels that automatically give saving grace.
catholic.sacraments: Catholics teach seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony. Sacraments are effective signs that give the grace they signify.
lds.sacraments: Latter-day Saints speak of ordinances, including saving ordinances such as baptism, confirmation, priesthood, endowment, and sealing. They are required covenants, not Catholic seven-sacrament language.
ortho.sacraments: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of Holy Mysteries. Baptism, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, unction, marriage, and orders are central, but they do not always lock the number at seven as a rigid system.
protestant.sacraments: Most Protestants recognize two sacraments or ordinances instituted by Christ: baptism and the Lord's Supper. Other rites may be valued without that rank.
baptist.real_presence: Baptists generally teach a memorial or symbolic presence: the bread and cup represent Christ's body and blood. Christ is present by his Spirit among believers, not in a change of the elements.
catholic.real_presence: Catholics teach the Real Presence by transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood, while appearances remain. Worship of the reserved sacrament follows from this.
lutheran.real_presence: Lutherans teach sacramental union or Real Presence: Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with, and under the bread and wine. They reject both mere symbolism and the Catholic explanation of transubstantiation.
ortho.real_presence: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach the Real Presence and a real change of the gifts into Christ's body and blood. They usually decline to define the change with the Latin philosophical term transubstantiation.
protestant.real_presence: Protestants range from memorial sign to spiritual feeding on Christ to Lutheran real presence. Lord's Supper presence is the shared question; answers differ.
reformed.real_presence: Reformed Christians teach a spiritual presence: the risen Christ is in heaven, yet believers truly feed on him by the Spirit through the supper. The bread remains bread; the communion is real, not empty.
catholic.eucharistic_sacrifice: Catholics teach the sacrifice of the Mass: the Eucharist makes present Christ's one sacrifice of the cross. It is not a new killing of Jesus, but the same offering represented and offered to the Father.
lutheran.eucharistic_sacrifice: Lutherans reject a propitiatory sacrifice of the Mass that adds to the cross. They may speak of a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving in the supper.
ortho.eucharistic_sacrifice: Eastern Orthodox Christians call the Divine Liturgy a bloodless sacrifice: the Church offers the consecrated gifts as Christ's once-for-all offering made present, not a repetition that improves Calvary.
protestant.eucharistic_sacrifice: Most Protestants treat the Lord's Supper as a memorial of the sacrifice, not a sacrifice that is offered again. Thanksgiving and remembrance are the key words.
baptist.closed_communion: Many Baptists practice close communion: the table is for baptized believers, sometimes only of their own church or of like faith and order. Open invitation to anyone present is not universal among them.
catholic.closed_communion: Catholics practice closed communion: ordinarily only Catholics in a state of grace receive. Sharing the Eucharist expresses already-existing full church communion.
lutheran.closed_communion: Confessional Lutherans practice closed communion or altar fellowship: those who share the same confessed faith commune together. It is about doctrine, not hospitality manners only.
ortho.closed_communion: Eastern Orthodox churches practice closed communion: the Eucharist is for the Orthodox who are prepared. Intercommunion with other churches is not normal practice.
protestant.closed_communion: Many Protestant churches practice open communion: all baptized believers, or all who trust Christ, are invited. Others keep a closer table. The Protestant world is split on the guest list.
adventist.foot_washing: Seventh-day Adventists practice the ordinance of humility, foot washing, before the Lord's Supper. It is a regular gospel ordinance of service and cleansing of attitude.
anabaptist.foot_washing: Some Anabaptist groups practice foot washing as an ordinance commanded by Jesus, a sign of humble service among members.
catholic.foot_washing: Catholics practice the mandatum, washing of feet, especially on Holy Thursday. It is a powerful liturgical sign, not one of the seven sacraments.
oneness_pentecostal.foot_washing: Some Oneness Pentecostal churches practice foot washing as an ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord's Supper, following Jesus' example in John 13.
catholic.temples: Catholics may call a church building a temple in a broad sense, but ordinary worship is in parish churches. The word temple does not name a separate class of restricted ritual buildings as in LDS usage.
community_of_christ.temples: Community of Christ has temples, notably at Independence and Kirtland, used for worship, peace, and learning. Their temple theology differs from LDS endowment and sealing practice.
lds.temples: Latter-day Saints build temples for sacred ordinances such as endowment and sealing, distinct from regular meetinghouses. Access is for members with a recommend, not for public Sunday services.
protestant.temples: Protestants usually say the body is the temple of the Holy Spirit and treat church buildings as meeting places. They do not have a separate LDS-style temple system.
anglican.liturgy: Anglicans are shaped by the Book of Common Prayer and ordered liturgy: set prayers, readings, and sacraments. Worship is corporate and scripted more than free-form.
catholic.liturgy: Catholics call public worship liturgy, especially the Mass in the Roman Rite and other rites. Official texts and actions are the Church's prayer, not only private devotion.
lutheran.liturgy: Lutherans often call Sunday worship the Divine Service: God serves the people through Word and sacrament in a structured liturgy with hymns and a sermon.
oriental_ortho.liturgy: Oriental Orthodox churches celebrate the Divine Liturgy or Holy Qurbana with ancient anaphoras. Worship is sacramental, sung, and inherited, not invented week by week.
ortho.liturgy: Eastern Orthodox Christians center worship in the Divine Liturgy. It is sung, iconic, and sacramental, understood as heaven and earth meeting.
protestant.liturgy: Protestants range from highly liturgical services to a simple order of worship built around singing, prayer, and a sermon. Liturgy here just means the shape of the service.
quaker.liturgy: Quakers classically practice waiting worship or a silent meeting: the congregation waits in silence until someone is moved to speak. There is no programmed Mass or set sacrament in traditional Friends practice.
catholic.prayer: Catholics pray in many forms: Mass, liturgy of the hours, rosary, spontaneous prayer, and contemplation. Prayer is addressed to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and also includes asking saints to intercede.
lds.prayer: Latter-day Saints pray to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ, usually in plain speech. Formal set liturgies are less central than in Catholic or Orthodox life.
ortho.prayer: Eastern Orthodox Christians practice liturgical prayer and personal prayer, including noetic prayer of the heart. Prayer is frequent, often using written prayers and the Jesus Prayer.
protestant.prayer: Protestants emphasize prayer as direct address to God, often informal. Written prayers exist, especially in liturgical churches, but many traditions prize free prayer in everyday words.
adventist.liturgical_calendar: Adventists do not treat the historic church year as binding. They debate biblical feasts and generally do not require a Catholic-style calendar of saints' days. Sabbath weekly time matters more than a festal cycle.
anglican.liturgical_calendar: Anglicans keep a church year: Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, Pentecost, and saints' days, structuring reading and worship.
catholic.liturgical_calendar: Catholics live by a liturgical year of seasons and feasts that retell the life of Christ and remember saints. The calendar shapes Mass readings and devotion.
ortho.liturgical_calendar: Eastern Orthodox Christians keep a rich liturgical year of fasts and feasts, including Pascha as the feast of feasts. Time itself is treated as a teacher of the gospel.
protestant.liturgical_calendar: Some Protestants keep a church calendar; others ignore it as unbiblical tradition. There is no single Protestant rule.
adventist.sabbath: Adventists teach the seventh-day Sabbath, Saturday, as still binding. Sunday is not the biblical Sabbath in their teaching.
catholic.sabbath: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, fulfilling the purpose of the Sabbath in honor of the Resurrection. Saturday rest as a binding Mosaic Sabbath is not required.
lds.sabbath: Latter-day Saints keep the Sabbath day on Sunday as a holy day of worship, rest, and covenant renewal, with detailed counsel about worthy Sunday activity.
messianic.sabbath: Messianic believers typically keep Shabbat on Friday evening through Saturday, following Jewish timing, as part of a Torah-positive following of Jesus.
protestant.sabbath: Protestants usually gather on the Lord's Day, Sunday. Some older Reformed voices called Sunday the Christian Sabbath; others say Sabbath was fulfilled and Sunday is a resurrection feast, not a relocated Saturday law.
seventh_day_adventist.sabbath: Seventh-day Adventists make Sabbath, Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, a central mark of faithfulness. It is both creation memorial and end-time sign in their teaching.
catholic.sunday_worship: Catholics teach a Sunday obligation: the faithful are to participate in Mass on Sunday and holy days. Sunday is the Lord's Day.
ortho.sunday_worship: Eastern Orthodox Christians treat Sunday as the Lord's Day, the weekly Pascha, when the Divine Liturgy is celebrated. It is the first day, the day of resurrection.
protestant.sunday_worship: Protestants generally worship on Sunday as the Lord's Day. Attendance expectations vary from solemn duty to voluntary gathering.
catholic.icons: Catholics use sacred images, statues, and icons as aids to devotion. Honoring an image is directed to the person depicted, not to wood or paint as a god.
oriental_ortho.icons: Oriental Orthodox churches use icons in worship and teaching. Images of Christ and the saints belong in church life.
ortho.icons: Eastern Orthodox Christians give a central place to holy icons. After the iconoclast controversies, they teach that images of Christ are possible because the Word became flesh. Icons are venerated, not worshiped as gods.
protestant.icons: Many Protestants are wary of images in worship, fearing idolatry. Some allow art for teaching; others strip churches of figures. Practice ranges from stained glass to bare walls.
reformed.icons: Classic Reformed teaching is severe about images in worship: God is not to be pictured for devotion, especially not the divine nature. Pictures of Jesus remain controversial in that stream.
catholic.veneration: Catholics distinguish veneration, dulia for saints and hyperdulia for Mary, from worship, latria, due to God alone. Bowing or lighting candles is honor, not the adoration given to God.
ortho.veneration: Eastern Orthodox Christians practice veneration or proskynesis toward icons and saints, while reserving true worship for God. The distinction is essential in their defense of icons.
protestant.veneration: Protestants often collapse veneration into worship of saints and reject it as unbiblical. Asking saints for prayer is commonly refused as taking honor that belongs to God or as unnecessary.
catholic.fasting: Catholics practice fasting and abstinence, especially in Lent and on certain Fridays. Rules have been simplified, but self-denial remains a communal discipline.
lds.fasting: Latter-day Saints keep Fast Sunday, usually the first Sunday of the month: going without food and drink for a period and giving a fast offering for the poor, with prayer.
oriental_ortho.fasting: Oriental Orthodox churches keep long and strict fasting seasons. Fasting is a normal part of church life, not an optional extra for the especially devout only.
ortho.fasting: Eastern Orthodox Christians fast often, above all in Great Lent: abstaining from certain foods as training of the body and soul. Fasting is communal and calendrical.
protestant.fasting: Protestants may fast as a personal spiritual practice. Few require a church-wide food calendar like the older churches.
catholic.sacred_music: Catholics treat sacred music, especially chant, as integral to liturgy. Many styles are now used, but the music is supposed to serve prayer, not replace it with a concert.
evangelical.sacred_music: Evangelicals often use contemporary worship songs as well as hymns. Music is a major vehicle of teaching and emotion in the gathering.
ortho.sacred_music: Eastern Orthodox worship uses chant and liturgical singing, traditionally without instruments in many churches. The human voice carries the prayers.
protestant.sacred_music: Protestants made hymns in the common tongue central. Worship music now includes everything from organ chorales to bands.
churches_of_christ.instrumental_music: Many Churches of Christ insist on a cappella worship: singing without instruments, because they find no New Testament command for instruments in church.
ortho.instrumental_music: Traditional Eastern Orthodox worship uses unaccompanied chant. Instruments are generally absent from the liturgy, though practice can vary in some places.
protestant.instrumental_music: Most Protestants accept instruments in worship as adiaphora, matters of freedom, unless a congregation chooses otherwise.
catholic.preaching: Catholics call the sermon a homily. It opens the readings and is part of the Mass, but the Eucharist, not the sermon, is the structural center.
ortho.preaching: Eastern Orthodox Christians include a homily in the liturgy. Preaching is important, yet the rite as a whole, not a long lecture, is the heart of Sunday.
protestant.preaching: Protestants typically make the sermon the climax of the service. Preaching the Word is the main event in many churches.
reformed.preaching: Reformed churches treat preaching of the Word as a means of grace: God himself addresses the congregation through Scripture explained and applied.
baptist.altar_call: Many Baptist churches give an invitation or call to come forward at the end of the sermon for conversion, baptism, or church membership.
evangelical.altar_call: Evangelicals popularized the altar call: an invitation to respond publicly to the gospel after preaching. It is a method, not a biblical ordinance required of all churches.
pentecostal.altar_call: Pentecostal services often end with an altar call for salvation, healing, or Spirit baptism. Coming to the front is a visible act of seeking God.
anglican.sign_of_the_cross: Many Anglicans make the sign of the cross in worship. It is permitted and traditional in that stream of Protestantism, not universal among all Protestants.
catholic.sign_of_the_cross: Catholics mark themselves with the sign of the cross: forehead, chest, shoulders, in the name of the Trinity. It is a brief creed in gesture.
lutheran.sign_of_the_cross: Lutherans historically retained the sign of the cross in devotion and liturgy. Luther commended it; usage varies by parish today.
oriental_ortho.sign_of_the_cross: Oriental Orthodox Christians make the sign of the cross, with local custom about finger position and direction. It is a constant act of faith.
ortho.sign_of_the_cross: Eastern Orthodox Christians sign themselves often, typically right to left, with the fingers arranged to confess the Trinity and the two natures of Christ.
anglican.rosary: Some Anglicans use an Anglican rosary, a different bead pattern from the Dominican Catholic rosary, as a help to repeated prayer. It is optional.
catholic.rosary: Catholics pray the Rosary: a set of beads and repeated prayers, especially Hail Mary, while meditating on events in the lives of Jesus and Mary. It is devotion, not a fourth person of the Trinity.
ortho.rosary: Eastern Orthodox Christians use a prayer rope, komboskini, to count the Jesus Prayer. It is not the same as the Catholic Marian rosary, though both use repetition as a tool.
catholic.jesus_prayer: Some Catholics use the Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, as a short repeated prayer borrowed from the East.
oriental_ortho.jesus_prayer: Oriental Orthodox Christians also know short repeated invocations of Jesus similar to the Jesus Prayer, as a way of continual repentance and remembrance of God.
ortho.jesus_prayer: Eastern Orthodox spirituality centers the Jesus Prayer, the prayer of the heart: a short cry for mercy repeated until it becomes inward attention to God.
catholic.mary: Catholics honor the Blessed Virgin Mary, Our Lady, as Mother of God and first among the saints. Honor of Mary is meant to serve Christ, not rival him.
lds.mary: Latter-day Saints honor Mary as the virgin mother of Jesus. She is not a focus of prayer or dogmas such as Immaculate Conception and Assumption in the Catholic sense.
oriental_ortho.mary: Oriental Orthodox churches honor Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God, in liturgy and feasts. She is central to devotion while remaining a creature.
ortho.mary: Eastern Orthodox Christians call Mary Theotokos, Panagia, all-holy, Mother of God. She is the model of the saved and is honored in every liturgy.
protestant.mary: Protestants honor Mary as the mother of Jesus and a model of faith, but most reject prayers to her and later Marian dogmas. She is a believer, not a mediator beside Christ in their usual teaching.
catholic.theotokos: Catholics confess Mary as Mother of God, Theotokos, because the one she bore is God the Son. The title protects the identity of Jesus, not an idea that Mary originated the Trinity.
church_of_the_east.theotokos: The Church of the East has preferred Christotokos, Mother of Christ, to guard the distinction of natures. In modern dialogue they explain this as not denying Christ's deity, but the older controversy was sharp.
oriental_ortho.theotokos: Oriental Orthodox churches confess Mary as Theotokos. The title is a pillar of their Christology: she bore the incarnate Word.
ortho.theotokos: Eastern Orthodox Christians treat Theotokos as nonnegotiable. To deny Mother of God is to split the one Christ.
protestant.theotokos: Some Protestants accept Mother of God as a true statement about Jesus' identity; others avoid it as sounding as if Mary is source of the Godhead and say only mother of Jesus.
catholic.immaculate_conception: Catholics define the Immaculate Conception: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception by grace from Christ. It is about Mary's beginning, not about Jesus' virgin birth.
ortho.immaculate_conception: Eastern Orthodox Christians honor Mary's holiness and often her personal sinlessness, but they typically reject the Catholic dogma of Immaculate Conception as a way of explaining it, because they do not share the same account of original guilt.
protestant.immaculate_conception: Protestants generally reject the Immaculate Conception as unbiblical. Mary needed a Savior like everyone else and was not conceived without original sin in their usual reading.
catholic.assumption: Catholics define the Assumption: Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory at the end of her earthly life. Whether she died first is left somewhat open in popular speech; the dogma affirms her bodily glorification.
oriental_ortho.assumption: Oriental Orthodox churches celebrate the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, and her being taken up. The feast is ancient; the Catholic 1950 definition is not their authority.
ortho.assumption: Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate the Dormition: Mary died and was raised and taken into heaven. They share the belief in her translation while rejecting the need for a papal definition.
protestant.assumption: Protestants generally reject the Assumption as a late dogma without biblical proof. Mary's end is left with God; it is not an article of faith for them.
catholic.perpetual_virginity: Catholics teach Mary's perpetual virginity: before, during, and after Jesus' birth she remained a virgin. Brothers of Jesus are read as relatives or kin, not sons of Mary.
lutheran.perpetual_virginity: Historic Lutheranism often affirmed Mary's perpetual virginity. Many modern Lutherans no longer emphasize it; the older confessional stream did.
ortho.perpetual_virginity: Eastern Orthodox Christians call Mary ever-virgin. The title is standard in liturgy. Brothers of the Lord are not treated as Mary's other children.
protestant.perpetual_virginity: Protestants divide. Many modern Protestants think the brothers of Jesus were Mary's later children and that perpetual virginity is unnecessary. Some Reformers still held it.
reformed.perpetual_virginity: Reformed Christians commonly read the brothers of the Lord as ordinary siblings. Perpetual virginity is not a Reformed dogma and is often denied.
catholic.intercession_of_saints: Catholics teach the intercession of saints: Christians may ask those in heaven to pray for them. This is praying to saints in the sense of addressing them, not worshiping them as God.
lds.intercession_of_saints: Latter-day Saints pray only to the Father in the name of Christ. They do not practice asking Mary or saints to intercede as in Catholic or Orthodox devotion.
oriental_ortho.intercession_of_saints: Oriental Orthodox churches ask the intercession of the saints in liturgy and private prayer. The departed righteous are alive to God and can be asked to pray.
ortho.intercession_of_saints: Eastern Orthodox Christians constantly ask the intercession of the saints, especially Mary. Icons and feast days structure this request for prayer.
protestant.intercession_of_saints: Most Protestants reject prayer to saints. The communion of saints means fellowship among believers, not a traffic of requests to the dead. Christ is the only mediator in their usual slogan.
catholic.relics: Catholics venerate relics, bodily remains or objects connected with saints, as honors to God's work in them and as occasions of prayer, not as magic charms in official teaching.
ortho.relics: Eastern Orthodox Christians honor holy relics, often placing them in altars and shrines. They are treated as bearers of holiness because the body shared in the Spirit's work.
protestant.relics: Protestants generally reject relic veneration as superstition or a distraction from faith in Christ. Reformers attacked relic trade as abuse.
catholic.prayers_for_the_dead: Catholics offer prayers for the dead, suffrages, especially in connection with purgatory: asking God to purify and help those who have died in grace but are not yet fully holy.
lds.prayers_for_the_dead: Latter-day Saints perform work for the dead, including baptism for the dead, so that the deceased may accept ordinances in the spirit world. This is vicarious covenant work, not only words of remembrance.
oriental_ortho.prayers_for_the_dead: Oriental Orthodox churches pray for the departed. Love and liturgy do not stop at death; the prayers commend the dead to God's mercy.
ortho.prayers_for_the_dead: Eastern Orthodox Christians pray for the departed at funerals and memorials. They do not define purgatory as Catholics do, but they refuse to treat the dead as beyond the Church's prayer.
protestant.prayers_for_the_dead: Most Protestants do not pray for the dead in order to change their state, believing the dead's destiny is fixed at death. Some Anglicans and others keep limited memorial prayers.
catholic.canonization_of_saints: Catholics canonize saints through an official process that permits public veneration of a person as among the blessed in heaven. It is a church judgment, not the making of a god.
ortho.canonization_of_saints: Eastern Orthodox Christians glorify saints: the Church recognizes holiness already present, often beginning with local veneration. There is no exact Roman legal process.
protestant.canonization_of_saints: Protestants typically say saints means all believers, not a special list of miracle-working dead. They may honor heroes of faith without an official canonization system.
catholic.heaven: Catholics teach heaven as the beatific vision: the blessed see God and are fully alive with him, awaiting the resurrection of the body. It is communion, not a vague cloud.
jehovahs_witnesses.heaven: Jehovah's Witnesses teach a heavenly hope for a little flock of 144,000 who will rule with Christ. Most of the righteous hope for life on a restored earth, not going to heaven.
lds.heaven: Latter-day Saints describe heaven in degrees, with the celestial kingdom as the highest presence of the Father. Heaven is differentiated, not a single identical reward.
ortho.heaven: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of heaven or paradise as life in God's presence and light. Language is often mystical: the same God is joy to the holy.
protestant.heaven: Protestants teach heaven as eternal life with God through Christ, often emphasizing being with the Lord and, finally, a new creation. Popular pictures of harps and clouds are not the doctrine.
catholic.hell: Catholics teach hell or Gehenna as the state of definitive self-exclusion from God, traditionally described as eternal punishment. It is the result of dying in unrepented mortal sin.
jehovahs_witnesses.hell: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Gehenna means destruction, not a place where immortal souls burn forever. They deny that the dead are conscious in fiery torment.
lds.hell: Latter-day Saints use hell for spirit prison and, in a final sense, outer darkness for the few who fully reject God after knowing him. Most people receive some degree of glory rather than endless torment.
ortho.hell: Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of hell or Hades. Some writers describe hell as the experience of God's love as torment for those who hate it. Official language still affirms a real, lasting ruin of the lost.
protestant.hell: Many Protestants teach hell as eternal punishment, conscious and unending. Others among them argue for annihilation. Classic evangelical preaching has emphasized eternal conscious torment.
anglican.purgatory: Anglicans have often spoken of an intermediate state while the official Reformation articles rejected Roman purgatory as taught then. Contemporary Anglicans range from rejection to cautious hope for continued purification.
catholic.purgatory: Catholics teach purgatory: those who die in God's friendship but still need purification are made holy after death before the fullness of heaven. It is not a second chance for the unrepentant.
ortho.purgatory: Eastern Orthodox Christians reject Catholic purgatory as a defined system of penal satisfaction. They speak of particular judgment, prayers for the dead, and sometimes popular images such as toll houses, which are not all equally official.
protestant.purgatory: Protestants generally reject purgatory as unbiblical and as undermining the completeness of Christ's work. The dead in Christ are with the Lord; others are not helped by Masses.
adventist.intermediate_state: Adventists teach that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. There is no aware intermediate life of souls in heaven or hell now.
catholic.intermediate_state: Catholics teach particular judgment at death: the soul goes to heaven, purgatory, or hell, awaiting the resurrection of the body.
lds.intermediate_state: Latter-day Saints teach a spirit world divided into paradise and prison, where the dead continue to learn and may accept the gospel before resurrection and final judgment.
ortho.intermediate_state: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach particular judgment and a state often called Hades or waiting, while the Church prays for the departed until the general resurrection.
protestant.intermediate_state: Many Protestants teach that believers are with the Lord at death, consciously, while awaiting bodily resurrection. That in-between is the intermediate state.
adventist.soul_sleep: Adventists teach soul sleep: the dead are unconscious, as asleep, until Christ raises them. Immortal-soul-in-heaven-at-once is rejected.
catholic.soul_sleep: Catholics teach an immortal soul that is judged at death and remains conscious. Soul sleep is rejected.
christadelphian.soul_sleep: Christadelphians teach the sleep of the dead: people are wholly dead until resurrection. There is no conscious immortal soul living on by nature.
jehovahs_witnesses.soul_sleep: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the dead are unconscious. The soul is the person; when the person dies, thought perishes until God resurrects.
protestant.soul_sleep: Most historic Protestants teach a conscious intermediate state, not soul sleep. A minority of Protestants agree with Adventist-style unconsciousness of the dead.
seventh_day_adventist.soul_sleep: Seventh-day Adventists make the state of the dead a landmark teaching: the dead know nothing until the resurrection. This supports their rejection of spiritualism and eternal torment of souls now.
catholic.resurrection_of_the_dead: Catholics teach the resurrection of the body: the same person is raised, transformed, at the end. Hope is not escape from the body as a ghost forever.
jehovahs_witnesses.resurrection_of_the_d: Jehovah's Witnesses teach resurrection, mostly to life on earth in a restored paradise. Heavenly resurrection is for the limited number who rule with Christ.
lds.resurrection_of_the_dead: Latter-day Saints teach a universal resurrection made possible by Christ, after which people are assigned to degrees of glory or, for a few, outer darkness.
ortho.resurrection_of_the_dead: Eastern Orthodox Christians confess the resurrection of the dead as a central hope. Pascha is the promise that all will rise.
protestant.resurrection_of_the_dead: Protestants teach the resurrection of the dead: believers raised to glory, the wicked to judgment. Christianity is not completed by an immortal soul alone.
adventist.last_judgment: Adventists include a distinctive pre-advent investigative judgment beginning in 1844, as well as final execution of judgment after the millennium.
catholic.last_judgment: Catholics distinguish particular judgment at death from the Last Judgment or general judgment, when all is publicly revealed and the risen are assigned their final place.
lds.last_judgment: Latter-day Saints teach a final judgment after resurrection, when each person is assigned a kingdom of glory or condemnation according to works and acceptance of Christ.
ortho.last_judgment: Eastern Orthodox Christians confess the Last Judgment as Christ's public verdict on all humanity. Icons of the judgment are common teaching tools.
protestant.last_judgment: Protestants teach a final judgment, often using the image of the great white throne. All people answer to Christ. Timing relative to a millennium varies.
adventist.investigative_judgment: Adventists teach a pre-advent judgment in which the heavenly records of professed believers are reviewed before Christ returns.
protestant.investigative_judgment: Most Protestants have no investigative judgment doctrine. Judgment is associated with Christ's return or with death, not with a 1844 heavenly review of books.
seventh_day_adventist.investigative_judg: Seventh-day Adventists uniquely teach the investigative judgment and heavenly sanctuary: in 1844 Christ began a final phase of ministry, examining the saints. This is a defining and contested doctrine.
adventist.second_coming: Adventists emphasize the soon Advent, the visible return of Christ, as a living hope that shapes life and mission.
catholic.second_coming: Catholics teach the Second Coming or Parousia: Christ will return in glory to judge and to complete the kingdom. Dates are not set.
lds.second_coming: Latter-day Saints teach a literal Second Coming of Christ to reign, preceded by signs, tribulation, and restoration events, including work in their temples and gathering.
ortho.second_coming: Eastern Orthodox Christians confess the Second Coming or Parousia in every creed and liturgy. Watchfulness, not calendar speculation, is the accent.
protestant.second_coming: Protestants teach the Second Coming or return of Christ as personal, visible, and decisive. Charts and timetables differ widely among them.
adventist.millennium: Adventists teach a millennium in which the righteous are with Christ and the earth is desolate, after which the final destruction of the wicked occurs.
catholic.millennium: Catholics officially reject a worldly thousand-year political reign of the saints before the end as a required hope. They are generally amillennial: the thousand years of Revelation is symbolic of the age of the Church.
evangelical.millennium: Evangelicals divide into premillennialism, Christ returns before a thousand-year reign; amillennialism, the thousand years is symbolic now; and postmillennialism, the gospel wins the world before he returns.
jehovahs_witnesses.millennium: Jehovah's Witnesses teach a literal thousand-year reign of Christ over the earth, during which the dead are raised and people learn obedience before a final test.
lds.millennium: Latter-day Saints teach a literal Millennium: Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years of peace, temples will operate, and Satan will be bound.
protestant.millennium: Protestants disagree about the thousand years in Revelation 20. The word millennium just means that disputed thousand-year period.
adventist.rapture: Adventists reject a secret rapture that removes the church while the world continues as usual. They teach one visible coming of Christ.
catholic.rapture: Catholics do not teach a pre-tribulation secret rapture as popular evangelical fiction does. The living faithful will meet Christ at his one glorious coming.
evangelical.rapture: Many evangelicals teach the rapture: believers are caught up to meet Christ. They disagree whether this happens before, during, or after a future tribulation.
protestant.rapture: Rapture language is especially evangelical Protestant. Other Protestants simply speak of being gathered to Christ at his return without a separate secret event.
adventist.annihilation: Adventists teach annihilation or conditional immortality: the lost are finally destroyed, not endlessly tortured. Immortality is a gift, not a natural property of the soul.
catholic.annihilation: Catholics teach eternal punishment. Official doctrine has not adopted annihilation of the damned as the Church's teaching, though the nature of that punishment is discussed.
jehovahs_witnesses.annihilation: Jehovah's Witnesses teach destruction of the wicked: they cease to exist. Eternal conscious torment is denied.
ortho.annihilation: Eastern Orthodox Christians traditionally teach eternal punishment. Annihilation is not the standard Orthodox confession, even when some writers use more paradoxical language about hell.
protestant.annihilation: Historic Protestantism taught eternal conscious torment. A growing minority of Protestants now defend annihilation or conditional immortality. The family is divided.
community_of_christ.degrees_of_glory: Community of Christ inherited language of degrees of glory from the early Latter Day Saint movement but does not emphasize the LDS three-kingdom map in the same official, salvific way today.
lds.degrees_of_glory: Latter-day Saints teach three degrees of glory—celestial, terrestrial, and telestial—plus outer darkness. Almost all people inherit a kingdom of glory after resurrection. This replaces a simple heaven-or-hell binary for most persons.
protestant.degrees_of_glory: Protestants typically teach one heaven for the saved and do not divide eternal reward into three kingdoms of glory as LDS scripture does. Rewards may differ; destinations are not mapped that way.
lds.spirit_world: Latter-day Saints teach that at death spirits go to a spirit world: paradise for the righteous, prison for others, where the gospel can be preached and choices continue until resurrection.
protestant.spirit_world: Protestants may speak of Hades or Sheol as the realm of the dead, but most do not teach an LDS-style missionary program among spirits. The next conscious state is with Christ or under judgment.
catholic.new_creation: Catholics hope for new heavens and a new earth: creation renewed, not discarded, when God is all in all and the risen live in a transformed world.
jehovahs_witnesses.new_creation: Jehovah's Witnesses hope for Paradise Earth: the planet restored to Eden-like peace for the great majority of the righteous, with a small number in heaven.
lds.new_creation: Latter-day Saints teach a renewed earth that will become the celestial kingdom for the highest saved. Creation's destiny is glory, not abandonment.
ortho.new_creation: Eastern Orthodox Christians hope for the new creation: the world transfigured by God's energies, matter made luminous, not escaped as if matter were evil.
protestant.new_creation: Protestants teach new heavens and a new earth as the final home of the righteous. Salvation is not only souls going upstairs forever.
catholic.marriage: Catholics teach marriage as the sacrament of Matrimony, a lifelong covenant between a man and a woman that signs Christ's union with the Church.
lds.marriage: Latter-day Saints teach eternal marriage or sealing in the temple: a covenant that can last beyond death and is required for the highest exaltation.
ortho.marriage: Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate marriage as a mystery of crowning. It is holy, monogamous in intent, and lived as a path of salvation, with limited pastoral exceptions for failure.
protestant.marriage: Protestants teach Christian marriage as a covenant before God, ordinarily lifelong between a man and a woman. It is honorable, but usually not called a sacrament in the Catholic sense.
catholic.divorce: Catholics teach the indissolubility of a valid sacramental marriage. Civil divorce does not free one to remarry in the Church. Annulment is a judgment that a true sacramental marriage never existed, not a Catholic word for divorce.
lds.divorce: Latter-day Saints permit civil divorce and, through church process, cancellation of sealing in some cases. The ideal remains eternal marriage; pastoral exceptions exist.
ortho.divorce: Eastern Orthodox churches permit divorce and remarriage in some cases by economia, pastoral condescension, treating the first crowning as the ideal and later marriages as penitential concessions.
protestant.divorce: Protestants generally allow divorce and remarriage in cases such as adultery or abandonment, with wide variation. Marriage is serious, but not always treated as absolutely indissoluble in the Catholic sense.
catholic.contraception: Catholics officially reject artificial birth control. They allow natural methods of spacing births. Sexual acts in marriage are to remain open to life in official teaching.
ortho.contraception: Eastern Orthodox teaching on contraception varies by bishop and church, often more pastoral than the Catholic ban, while still treating children as a blessing and rejecting an anti-life mindset.
protestant.contraception: Most Protestants accept birth control within marriage as a matter of prudence. Some conservative groups dissent. There is no single Protestant rule.
catholic.abortion: Catholics teach that abortion is the taking of innocent human life and is gravely wrong from conception. This is among their most emphasized moral teachings.
evangelical.abortion: Most evangelicals oppose abortion as the unjust taking of unborn human life. The issue is a major public marker of evangelical ethics in many countries.
ortho.abortion: Eastern Orthodox Christians condemn abortion as the taking of life. Canon law historically imposed serious penances. The unborn are treated as persons to be protected.
protestant.abortion: Historic Protestant teaching opposed abortion. Today Protestant bodies range from strictly opposed to permissive. The word names the moral dispute, not one verdict.
catholic.sexual_ethics: Catholics teach chastity for all states of life: sex belongs in marriage between man and woman, open to life. Sexual morality is detailed in official teaching.
evangelical.sexual_ethics: Evangelicals typically teach biblical sexual ethics: sex within male-female marriage, abstinence outside it. Same-sex practice and pornography are widely rejected in official evangelical statements.
lds.sexual_ethics: Latter-day Saints teach the law of chastity: no sexual relations outside marriage between a man and a woman. The standard is a major membership expectation.
ortho.sexual_ethics: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach chastity and reserve sexual union for marriage of man and woman. Fasting seasons also shape marital practice in traditional discipline.
protestant.sexual_ethics: Protestants historically taught sex within marriage and chastity outside it. Contemporary Protestants are sharply divided on several sexual questions.
adventist.tithing: Adventists teach tithe, a tenth of income, as a continuing biblical duty for supporting ministry, with offerings beyond the tithe.
catholic.tithing: Catholics teach stewardship and offerings to support the Church. A strict 10 percent tithe is not enforced as divine law in the same way as in some Protestant or LDS settings.
evangelical.tithing: Many evangelicals teach tithing as a biblical baseline of giving, though some say New Testament giving is free and generous rather than a fixed tenth.
lds.tithing: Latter-day Saints treat tithing as a commandment and a requirement for a temple recommend: a tenth of increase given to the church.
protestant.tithing: Protestants speak of giving and stewardship. Some insist on the tithe; others teach cheerful, proportional giving without making 10 percent a law.
adventist.alcohol: Adventists teach temperance as abstinence from alcohol. Health teaching is part of discipleship, not only private preference.
catholic.alcohol: Catholics teach temperance: alcohol may be used moderately. Drunkenness is a sin; wine is used in the Mass.
holiness.alcohol: Holiness churches often require total abstinence from alcohol as a mark of a sanctified life.
lds.alcohol: Latter-day Saints follow the Word of Wisdom, which forbids alcohol. Obedience is part of temple worthiness.
protestant.alcohol: Protestants range from moderation, including wine at Communion, to total abstinence. There is no single Protestant rule.
anabaptist.pacifism: Anabaptists classically teach nonresistance or pacifism: disciples do not take up the sword. The church is a peaceful minority, not a chaplain to war.
catholic.pacifism: Catholics officially allow just war under strict conditions while also honoring pacifism as a possible vocation. War is not a good, but it is not always forbidden.
mennonite.pacifism: Mennonites emphasize a peace witness: refusing military violence and working for reconciliation as a church identity, not an optional extra.
protestant.pacifism: Protestants include both just war majorities and pacifist minorities. The tradition does not speak with one voice on war and peace.
quaker.pacifism: Quakers hold a peace testimony: refusal of war as incompatible with the Spirit of Christ. It is a historic mark of Friends.
baptist.church_and_state: Baptists historically championed separation of church and state and soul liberty: the civil government should not coerce faith. The church is a voluntary community.
catholic.church_and_state: Catholics have taught various models of church and state, from older integral arrangements to modern religious freedom. The Church claims spiritual independence from the state.
lds.church_and_state: Latter-day Saints officially teach political neutrality of the church as an institution while encouraging civic engagement. Church and state are distinct in current practice.
ortho.church_and_state: Eastern Orthodox history often speaks of symphony between church and empire: distinct roles in a Christian society. Modern Orthodox churches live under many kinds of states.
protestant.church_and_state: Protestants have included state churches and strict separatists. The Reformation did not produce one political theology.
anabaptist.oaths: Anabaptists often refuse oaths, citing Jesus' command to let yes be yes. Simple truthful speech replaces swearing.
catholic.oaths: Catholics allow oaths in court and public life when truth and justice require them. False or vain oaths are sins.
protestant.oaths: Most Protestants accept lawful oaths. A minority follow the Anabaptist or Quaker refusal.
quaker.oaths: Quakers refuse oaths and use affirmation instead. Swearing is seen as implying a double standard of truth.
adventist.food_laws: Adventists teach a health message that includes avoiding unclean meats as in Leviticus, plus broader counsel on diet. Food is a discipleship issue.
jehovahs_witnesses.food_laws: Jehovah's Witnesses require abstaining from blood, including certain medical uses of blood, based on Acts 15. Other Mosaic food laws are not generally binding.
lds.food_laws: Latter-day Saints follow the Word of Wisdom: no alcohol, tobacco, coffee, or tea, and counsel toward wholesome food. It is a modern health revelation, not a full kosher system.
messianic.food_laws: Many Messianic believers keep kashrut or some biblical food laws as part of covenant faithfulness, while differing on how much of rabbinic kosher they adopt.
protestant.food_laws: Most Protestants teach that all foods are clean in Christ. Dietary rules are matters of health or preference, not salvation.
baptist.ordination_of_women: Baptists divide: some conventions bar women pastors; others ordain women freely. Local church polity makes the practice uneven.
catholic.ordination_of_women: Catholics teach a male-only priesthood: the Church has no authority to ordain women as priests or bishops. This is presented as a definitive no in official teaching.
lds.ordination_of_women: Latter-day Saints do not ordain women to priesthood offices in current practice. Women lead in other organizations and participate in some temple ordinances; priesthood office remains male.
methodist.ordination_of_women: Many Methodist bodies practice women's ordination and have women bishops. It is a settled yes in large Wesleyan denominations, though not in every Holiness offshoot.
ortho.ordination_of_women: Eastern Orthodox churches do not ordain women as priests or bishops. Discussion of female deacons exists; priestly ordination is not accepted practice.
protestant.ordination_of_women: Protestants are split on women in ministry. Some see ordination of women as gospel equality; others see it as barred by New Testament office texts.
catholic.headship: Catholics speak of complementarity: men and women are equal in dignity with distinct roles, especially in priesthood and, in official teaching, in family order.
evangelical.headship: Evangelicals are divided between complementarianism, male headship in home and church, and egalitarianism, shared authority. Headship is a live dispute, not a single evangelical dogma.
lds.headship: Latter-day Saints teach that a husband presides in the home in righteousness, as a partner with his wife, not as a tyrant. Priesthood and family government are linked in their language.
ortho.headship: Eastern Orthodox Christians traditionally teach a form of headship in family and church order while confessing equal dignity. Practice and tone vary by culture.
protestant.headship: Protestants debate roles of men and women using headship texts in Paul. There is no united Protestant position.
anabaptist.head_covering: Many conservative Anabaptists require a prayer covering or head covering for women in worship and often daily, reading 1 Corinthians 11 as standing practice.
catholic.head_covering: Catholics once commonly used a chapel veil or mantilla in church. It is no longer required in the Latin Church, though some women still wear it.
ortho.head_covering: In many Eastern Orthodox parishes women cover the head in church. Custom varies by country and parish; it is piety and order more than a defined worldwide dogma.
protestant.head_covering: Most modern Protestants do not require head covering. A minority of congregations still treat 1 Corinthians 11 as a present command.
community_of_christ.mormon_label: Community of Christ, once RLDS, has distanced itself from the nickname Mormon. The label is historically related but is not their preferred name.
lds.mormon_label: Latter-day Saints now prefer Latter-day Saint rather than Mormon or Mormon Church. Mormon remains a widely known nickname and the name of their distinctive book.
protestant.mormon_label: Protestants commonly say Mormon for Latter-day Saints. The word is an outsider label that bundles doctrine, culture, and the Book of Mormon.
catholic.roman_catholic_label: Catholics usually call themselves Catholic, meaning universal. Roman Catholic specifies communion with the bishop of Rome and the Latin tradition; they often find Roman Catholic used by others to imply they are only one sect among catholics.
ortho.roman_catholic_label: Eastern Orthodox Christians often say Roman Catholic or Latins for the Western church in communion with Rome. Catholic by itself, for them, properly belongs to the Orthodox Church's creed.
protestant.roman_catholic_label: Protestants commonly say Roman Catholic or Catholic interchangeably for the church headed by the pope. The adjective Roman marks difference from their own claim to belong to the universal church.
catholic.separated_brethren: Catholics since the mid-twentieth century call other baptized Christians separated brethren: truly Christian in important ways, yet not in full communion. Older language was harsher.
evangelical.separated_brethren: Evangelicals may speak of other believers, or of nominal Christians when they doubt that church membership equals conversion. The line is drawn around a living gospel faith more than around a denomination name.
ortho.separated_brethren: Eastern Orthodox Christians often call non-Orthodox heterodox. They may recognize baptism or good faith in others without treating them as the Church in the full sense.
protestant.separated_brethren: Protestants speak of other denominations as fellow Christians with whom they disagree. The tone ranges from partnership to sharp warning.
catholic.true_church_claim: Catholics identify the Catholic Church with the Church Christ founded. Fullness of means of salvation is there; other communities share elements of that Church.
iglesia_ni_cristo.true_church_claim: Iglesia ni Cristo claims to be the true Church of Christ, restored in the last days. Other churches are not accepted as that church.
lds.true_church_claim: Latter-day Saints claim to be the only true and living church, meaning unique authority and fullness, not that every other believer is insincere.
ortho.true_church_claim: Eastern Orthodox Christians identify the Orthodox Church as the one holy catholic and apostolic Church. Unity means entering that faith and communion.
restorationist.true_church_claim: Restorationists claim to recover the New Testament church itself rather than to be one more denomination. The true church is the restored original pattern.
